node_definition.done_when: Read design/canvas-layout-spec.md for type scale and spacing, but note the canvas topbar was drawn against a three-project fixture and cannot hold twelve, so this departs from it deliberately on the lead's instruction. FIVE PARTS, one node because the whole point is that one preference propagates — splitting this across files is what produced the r-3col defect earlier today, where a container's rules were retired in one scope and the container survived in another. ONE: the topbar becomes a single row — brand, project control, tabs, search, settings, snapshot receipt — with the tabs left-aligned after the project control. TWO: the Overview tab is removed. The brand button already calls navProject(null) titled All projects and renders the fleet page, and CockpitBody renders the same cross-project content, so they are two doors to one room; fold anything CockpitBody shows that the fleet view does not into the fleet view rather than dropping it, and leave the tabs as the four within-project views Plans, Sprints, Graph and Crew. THREE: the project control shows the current project with its live dot and opens a dropdown listing only VISIBLE projects, each with its plan count and live count, plus a Configure entry at the foot. FOUR: Configure opens the visibility panel that lives in the settings menu in docs/ui/_shared.jsx beside theme and density, which already own exactly this class of cross-cutting display preference — the dropdown entry is a shortcut that opens that same panel and must not be a second implementation of it. The panel lists every mounted project with a visible or hidden toggle. FIVE: visibility propagates. It is read today only by shell.jsx for the chip strip; crew.jsx and the fleet strip never see it. Every fleet-wide display must respect it: the Crew run list, the Overview fleet statistics, and any other cross-project aggregate. Distinguish mounted from shown where a count is displayed, since twelve mounted and three shown are different facts. CRITICAL AND SUBTLE: hidden means excluded from aggregates and from the selector shortcut list; it must never mean unreachable. Any mounted project stays reachable through Configure and through the command palette — a project being hidden is why nova could not be selected, and that bug is a display preference wrongly used as a routing filter. A test asserts the topbar renders one row containing the tabs with no Overview tab, that the dropdown lists visible projects only and offers Configure, that Configure and the settings menu render the same panel rather than two, that hiding a project removes it from the Crew list and the fleet statistics while leaving it selectable through the palette, and that a count displaying mounted and shown reports both. The existing suite passes unchanged.
node_definition.goal: Make project visibility one fleet-wide setting that every surface respects, and fit the topbar on one row

That staleness heuristic is right for a manifest written mid-run and then superseded, but it is wrong for a TERMINAL status: complete, blocked and failed are facts a later log line cannot undo, and discarding them is what erases the strongest completion signal available. node_definition.done_when: reckon/crew/promotion.py appends the ledger row and deletes the live pointer, in that order so an interruption stays recoverable, and releases nothing else: the run's worktree survives until someone runs crew gc by hand and the worker process survives until it exits on its own. Measured on this workstation: 274 worktrees on disk against 458 promoted runs in one ledger, and a run observed process_alive true while its classification already read completed_unpromoted. Extend complete so that AFTER the ledger append and the pointer delete it also releases the run's own worktree and, if still alive, the run's own process group. Reuse the classification crew gc already applies in reckon/crew/routing.py rather than writing a second policy: a worktree is released only when git status --porcelain in it reports zero entries AND its HEAD is an ancestor of the integration branch as git merge-base --is-ancestor decides; a worktree failing either condition is left in place and never removed with force; and a shadow releases through the existing lineage rule against its committed record and retained patch. The process group is signalled only when a terminal manifest was delivered, because a live process with no manifest is a recovery case rather than a cleanup one. Every withheld release is named in the returned completion result with the condition it failed, so a retained worktree is visible at the moment it is created rather than discovered by a later path collision. A failure inside the release step must never undo or obscure the ledger append. Tests in tests/test_promotion_release.py assert: a promoted run whose worktree reports zero porcelain entries and whose HEAD is an ancestor of the integration branch leaves no worktree on disk and no live process, asserted through complete end to end rather than by unit-testing a helper; a promoted run whose worktree reports a porcelain entry keeps that worktree and names it in the result with the failed condition; one whose HEAD is not an ancestor of the integration branch does the same; a run with no terminal manifest is never signalled; and a simulated failure raised inside the release step still leaves the promoted ledger row intact and the run recoverable. Your gate is that new file plus tests/test_crew_promotion.py, tests/test_crew_promotion_scope.py and tests/test_crew_gc.py. Do NOT run the full suite and do NOT run any browser-driven test. node_definition.done_when: Two sessions independently watched finished runs display as working: one saw six nodes whose worker processes had all exited and whose manifests were all terminal on disk sit as '6 working' for 38 minutes with zero events, and one saw a run whose classifier read completed_unpromoted with a complete manifest while its phase still read starting. The mechanism is in reckon/crew/recovery.py and has two parts that compound. First, in classify_pointer around lines 186 to 196, when the process appears alive AND the log file's mtime is newer than the manifest's, the manifest is discarded wholesale: manifest_present set false, manifest_data emptied, manifest_status set to empty string. That staleness heuristic is right for a manifest written mid-run and then superseded, but it is wrong for a TERMINAL status: complete, blocked and failed are facts a later log line cannot undo, and discarding them is what erases the strongest completion signal available. Second, in _watch_snapshot around lines 556 to 578, state resolves to dispatched when phase is starting and the stall check that follows is gated on state being exactly working, while FLEET_WORKING_STATES at line 610 counts dispatched among the working bucket. So a run that dies before its phase advances is counted as alive and is permanently ineligible for the stall check. Fix both, leading with the manifest because it turns a timing question into a fact-on-disk question: never discard a terminal manifest status through the staleness path, and evaluate the stall check over every non-terminal state rather than working alone. Tests in tests/test_crew_finished_display.py assert: a pointer whose manifest reports complete while its log is newer and its process appears alive still resolves to a terminal state rather than dispatched, and the same for blocked and failed; a run killed immediately after dispatch, before its phase ever advances past starting, is still detected from its manifest alone; a run with no manifest and no activity past the stall window resolves to stalled from the dispatched state, which it cannot today; and a genuinely mid-run pointer whose manifest is non-terminal and whose log is newer still has that manifest treated as superseded, so the staleness heuristic is narrowed rather than removed. Your gate is that new test file plus tests/test_crew_recovery.py, tests/test_crew_ticker.py and tests/test_crew_watch_stream.py. Do NOT run the full suite and do NOT run any browser-driven test. Judge by delta against base 937c2169a873d4e91102a5c5465cdca057788350

node_definition.done_when: Everything landed against this failure so far is defence: a promotion that would delete a resume path is refused, the hold ages from its refusal, the shelf life is configurable. A lane whose hold is still in force is never resumed onto, so the sweep cannot spend the last of a recovering quota. Measured tonight from this repository's committed ledger, data.holds: a claude dispatch hold opened 20:02:18Z and closed 23:52:19Z, held_seconds 13801, three hours fifty minutes on a lane that was serving. The control sits beside it - a claude-opus resume hold, held_seconds 83, closed the moment one served run reached that backend. The two differ only in whether traffic reached that specific backend. Every refused resume re-stamps the backend's budget record, so a caller retrying on any cadence shorter than the shelf life pushes the expiry ahead of itself, and observing the refused run does the same because its stream carries the rejection - the obvious check-before-believing move makes it worse. A served probe clears the hold and records the served observation so the next caller reads a fact rather than repeating the probe; a refused probe re-arms the hold and records that refusal as the new evidence. node_definition.done_when: A crew follow process holds the module code it imported for its entire life. When a recovery sweep landed and was wired into that loop, every follower on this workstation had started hours earlier, so not one called it - two independent sessions were simultaneously unable to perform a recovery they had just gained, and one left a run blocked five hours forty-two minutes with its limit long lifted. The failure is silent in the costly direction: a stale renderer draws a wrong column and someone notices, while a stale follower recovers nothing and is indistinguishable from a fleet with nothing to recover. THREE SHAPES IN THE ORDER TO TRY THEM, and the plan states this order deliberately. First, the follower detects that the installed package on disk is newer than the one it imported and re-execs itself in place, preserving its session registration and its stdout so a watching pane sees no gap. Second, if in-place re-exec cannot preserve those, the watch seat publishes a version stamp each cycle and a follower reading a stamp newer than its own re-execs. Third, only if neither is achievable, the follower emits one line saying it is stale and how to cycle it - this is a fallback, not the answer, because the done-when requires an operator who never restarts a follower to still get new behaviour. BOTH PRICES ARE PAID IN THE CURRENCY THIS SYSTEM SPENT THE NIGHT PROTECTING: manual worktree removal is the act that turned a ten-minute provider outage into a loss of five recoverable sessions, and crew complete now refuses to promote a blocked run whose session is recoverable precisely to prevent it - so the switching path routes a careful operator toward the one action the rest of the system guards against. THE DEFECT, reproduced here at this head against reckon/crew/reports.py _parse_text_manifest: line 98 does line = raw.strip() BEFORE applying the key regex, so an indented two-space commits key matches exactly like a column-0 key and overwrites it. _is_block_indicator called on an empty string returns False, so a parent key such as failure_attribution with an empty value never opens a block and every nested key under it is parsed as top level. Reproduced in three manifest shapes, all overwriting. An imas-codex fleet measured the cost today on run r-20260905T120506861337-n-sli-the-timestamp-work-did-not-add-failures: its manifest carried commits ["1ea93df8a"] at column 0 on line 7 and a nested commits ["94d31af9f", "57155c6e6"] on line 72 under failure_attribution, naming the commits the node was INVESTIGATING. crew live and crew drain both reported that nested pair as manifest_commits, and the rendered next action offered --commit ["94d31af9f" --commit "57155c6e6"]. A coordinator followed that instruction and committed ledger row 87db3c86c citing two wrong SHAs. So the bug is worse than a misparse: the surface renders a wrong value into a command it presents as runnable, and it bites precisely the manifests that do failure attribution properly. A second sub-defect is visible in that same rendering — a JSON list value is split on commas without stripping brackets or quotes, so the elements retain a leading bracket and quote characters, which is how the bracket reached the command. Those are handled today by the branch matching a stripped line that starts with a hyphen or asterisk, and they must keep working. So distinguish an indented list ITEM, which continues the current key, from an indented KEY line, which must not become a top-level key. Assert all of it: the top-level value wins over a nested one; an indented list item still appends to its key; a bracketed list parses to bare SHAs with no bracket or quote character left in any element; and the next action string built from those commits contains no bracket character. node_definition.done_when: pytest tests/test_local_lane_refusal_signal.py -q passes, and a stream that died of rate limiting no longer reports that it carries no rate-limit event. THE DEFECT, measured tonight across four dead runs in two projects: reckon/_backends.py line 852 reads exactly one record kind for budget, "elif kind == rate_limit_event", and nothing in that module reads api_retry or error_status. The clive local backend never emits rate_limit_event. It emits api_retry records carrying error_status 429 and error rate_limit. So a run that died of rate limiting is recorded with budget detail "no rate-limit event in the stream yet", refusal false, headroom unknown. The documented rule is that unknown headroom never holds a wave, and correctly so, which means the fence cannot fire at any level of local exhaustion and the next wave dispatches into the lane that just shed workers. This is a guard that cannot fire, which outranks a guard that fires wrongly: a stale hold announces itself while a blind one is indistinguishable from a clear lane. THE SHAPES, measured rather than assumed. Exhaustion: many api_retry records then a terminal result record carrying subtype success together with is_error true. Mid-flight death: api_retry records and no terminal result record at all. DO NOT key on a retry count of ten. Ten is the retry budget for a single API call, not for a run; two dead runs here carry 15 and 18 api_retry records and two in another project carry 10 and 5, so any constant matches some exhaustions and misses others, which is the worst behaviour available to a fence. Read the count as a magnitude and the terminal shape as the verdict. THE FALSIFIER, and it is the assertion that matters most: retrying is not refusing. Two runs that completed normally tonight each carried SEVEN api_retry records and finished with real work committed. A change that treats any api_retry as a refusal would mark every busy lane spent and hold the whole fleet, and it would pass any test that only checks the dead runs. Assert both directions: a stream with retries that ends in a genuine success reports no refusal and does not hold; a stream whose retries end in the exhaustion shape reports a refusal with a stated reason naming rate limiting; a stream with no retries at all is unchanged; and the existing rate_limit_event path for other backends keeps working exactly as it does now. Measure base and head over tests/test_local_lane_refusal_signal.py plus every test importing reckon._backends; report failure ids either side and require none added.
node_definition.goal: Teach the budget observer to see the exhaustion signal the local lane actually writes, so a spent local lane can be known before the next wave enters it

node_definition.done_when: pytest tests/test_closure_fence_agreement.py -q passes, and no pointer is reconciled on one surface and unreconciled on the other. THE DEFECT, measured by an imas-codex fleet and confirmed here at the source: two independent definitions of one word, neither consulting the other. reckon/crew/runs.py drain, around line 823, treats a pointer as reconciled when its recorded closure_disposition is handed-off, or still-working while its classification is running; for handed-off it consults neither age nor classification, and its docstring states that intent plainly, that a handoff remains valid until the receiving session reconciles the pointer. reckon/crew/recovery.py overdue_unreconciled_runs, around line 873, treats a pointer as unreconciled when its classification is completed_unpromoted or blocked and its terminal age exceeds the configured grace, and it never reads closure_disposition at all. So a terminal pointer past grace carrying a valid handed-off disposition is reconciled by drain and refused by dispatch with exit 6. That fleet measured exactly this on three pointers at once. WHY IT IS NOT A DISPLAY NIT: the ship skill instructs a coordinator to read the drain view and require unreconciled-runs zero before ending a session, so the fence a closure signature rests on is the permissive one. Their outgoing coordinator signed a sprint closure on that zero and committed it, attesting to a state the other surface denies. A fence satisfiable on one surface and refused on the other is not a fence. THE FIX: have overdue_unreconciled_runs consult the same recorded disposition drain does, through one shared predicate both call, so the two agree by construction rather than by two authors agreeing. Do not simply widen dispatch to ignore the pointers. THE PROTECTION THAT MUST SURVIVE, and these are the load-bearing assertions: a terminal pointer past grace carrying NO disposition is still refused by dispatch, because that is the forgotten-work case the fence exists for; a still-working disposition on a pointer that has since gone terminal excuses nothing on either surface, since drain already expires that and dispatch must not become the weaker of the two; and a handed-off pointer is reconciled on BOTH surfaces. Assert additionally that for a set of pointers mixing all three cases, the count drain reports and the count dispatch refuses on are equal. A change that merely relaxes dispatch would pass the third assertion and destroy the first. Measure base and head over tests/test_closure_fence_agreement.py plus every test importing reckon.crew.recovery or reckon.crew.runs; report failure ids either side and require none added.
node_definition.goal: Make the closure fence and the dispatch fence read one definition of unreconciled, so a session cannot be closed on a state dispatch denies

node_definition.done_when: pytest tests/test_lane_concurrency_ceiling.py -q passes, and a dispatch to a backend already carrying its ceiling of live runs is refused with a named, actionable reason instead of launching. The mechanism is not ours to fix downstream: the harness retry budget is fixed at max_retries 10 with 5 to 39 second backoff, reckon passes no retry configuration and cannot extend it, so once a lane refuses long enough the turn errors and a print-mode process exits. A 429 is a pause at the protocol; the finite retry budget is what converts it into a death. Therefore the only reliable remedy is not to create the overload. node_definition.done_when: pytest tests/test_review_scoring.py -q passes, and the four artefacts below exist and are exercised by that file. WHY THIS EXISTS. A promoted run today carries a gate the worker wrote itself, which is why gate pass sits at 1.00 on every lane in the committed ledger and cannot separate one lane from another. An independent reader of the landed diff, run before the promotion decision rather than after it, supplies a second opinion the worker did not author. The local lane has the throughput to run one per landing. WHAT TO BUILD, all of it new files, none of it wired into dispatch or promotion in this node. FIRST, a persisted prompt file at reckon/crew/prompts/review.md holding the text a review worker is given. It is a file rather than a string inside a module so that it is versioned, diffable, and editable without a code change. It instructs the reviewer to read the source node goal, its done_when, its declared write paths, its manifest, and the diff of its commits against its base, and to emit one score from 0 to 20 for each of five named dimensions together with one sentence of justification per dimension citing a path or a line, plus a list of findings each naming a file and a line. The five dimensions are goal_fidelity, meaning the landed change does what the node goal states; evidence, meaning the gate measures what the done_when asserts and its result is recorded; scope_discipline, meaning the diff stays inside the declared write paths and carries nothing the goal does not imply; durability, meaning a test exists that fails if this change regresses; and fit, meaning the change matches the idiom of the code around it and introduces no name the repository naming rules forbid. SECOND, a schema in reckon/crew/review.py naming those five dimensions once, with the maximum of 20 stated once, so that a dimension added later is added in one place. THIRD, a parser in the same module turning a review worker emitted text into that schema. It accepts the emitted form the prompt asks for. It returns a value for every dimension the schema names. It does not average, weight, rank, or compare lanes; the total it reports is the arithmetic sum of what it parsed and nothing else. FOURTH, a durable store in the same module writing one review record per reviewed run under the reckon crew configuration directory, outside any run directory and outside any worktree, keyed by project and by the reviewed run id, with a read function returning it. The location must survive deletion of the run directory and of the worktree, because a measure that reads a file the cleaner removes decays to nothing. Every record carries the reviewed run id, the review run id, the reviewing backend and model, the timestamp, the parsed scores, the justifications, the findings, and the verbatim emitted text it parsed, so a later reader can re-derive the parse and see what was actually said. DO NOT WIRE IT. This node writes no call site in dispatch, promotion, recovery, or the ticker; those files are held by other workers in flight. It exposes the functions those call sites will use and nothing more. FALSIFIERS, each asserted in the test file. Emitted text missing one dimension parses to a record naming that dimension as absent, not to a total computed over four, because a total silently taken over fewer dimensions is a lower score indistinguishable from a worse one. A score outside 0 to 20 is refused with a message naming the dimension and the value rather than being clamped into range. Emitted text that does not parse at all is stored with its verbatim text and a status saying it did not parse, because an unparsed review and an absent review are different facts and merging them is the failure this store exists to prevent. A record written and then read back through the read function is equal to what was written. The store path resolves under the configuration directory the test points at a temporary location and the test asserts the real configuration directory gained no file. The prompt file is loaded from disk at call time and the test asserts the loaded text contains each of the five dimension names, so a dimension renamed in the schema and not in the prompt is caught. Measure base and head over tests/test_review_scoring.py and every test importing reckon.crew.prompts; report failure ids either side and require none added.

A second project measured codex-spark at that time returning a hard usage-limit refusal naming its own reset, after four of its runs died at their first turn with no thread recorded. So the lane that was refusing reported 95 percent of its quota remaining, and a coordinator reading the preflight dispatched into it. THE MECHANISM. The account surface is read once and attributed to every backend whose name begins with the family prefix. The three named lanes have no state of their own, so the shared reading is the only thing describing them. Note what this does to a repair made elsewhere: a refusal parser that learns to read a hard usage-limit message would write that refusal against one of those names, and the next preflight would overwrite it from the shared surface, because the surface describes a different lane. The attribution defect therefore outranks the parser defect, and fixing the parser alone leaves the wrong verdict standing. WHAT TO CHANGE. A reading carries the identity of the lane it was observed on and is applied to that lane alone. Where one account surface genuinely covers several backends, that coverage is declared rather than inferred from a name prefix. A backend covered by no reading reports headroom unknown. Unknown is not held, matching this module's existing treatment of a window that has rolled over, and for the reason recorded there: only a served run writes a fresh budget record, so a hold derived from an absent signal has no path back. WHAT NOT TO CHANGE. Do not alter the ceiling, the resume reserve, the burn floors, or the projected exhaustion path landed earlier today. Do not change how any single reading is parsed or aged; this node changes which backends a reading speaks for and nothing else. FALSIFIERS, each asserted in tests/test_budget_evidence_scope.py against constructed states rather than a live account. A reading observed on one backend leaves every other backend reporting unknown, asserted over a family of four sharing a name prefix, so the measured shape above is refused by the result. A backend reporting unknown is not held. A declared multi-backend coverage applies to exactly the backends it names and to no others, and a backend absent from that declaration is unknown rather than covered. A backend that has its own reading keeps its own verdict unchanged, held or clear, so this removes attribution without altering any lane's own judgement. The nine backends this project configures each resolve to exactly one reading or to none, asserted by identity of the reading rather than by equality of its values, because two lanes that genuinely read the same numbers must still be distinguishable from one lane read twice. Measure base and head over tests/test_budget_evidence_scope.py and every test importing reckon.budget; report failure ids either side and require none added.

node_definition.done_when: pytest tests/test_resume_reaps_its_child.py -q passes, and a worker launched by the resume-ready sweep leaves no defunct child behind when it finishes. MEASURED ON A LIVE FLEET AND RECURRING, NOT A ONE-OFF. A peer session runs crew follow, whose loop performs the resume-ready sweep on a cadence. Every run that sweep wakes ends as a Z child of the follower when its turn finishes, and the NEXT crew resume on that run is then refused with "still has a live process; observe or stop it before resuming". Observed twice on the same run, at 13:33Z and again at 13:57Z. Their workaround is to stop the follower, resume, and re-arm — dropping their live view each time. So the declared-wait recovery path works and then poisons the next recovery of the same run. THE MECHANISM: reckon/crew/dispatch.py around line 2404 launches the worker with subprocess.Popen and start_new_session=True. start_new_session detaches the child into its own session and process group but does NOT reparent it — the spawning process still owes a wait. For an ordinary crew dispatch the CLI exits moments later, the child reparents to init and is reaped, and nobody notices. For a LONG-LIVED parent — a follower whose sweep launches resumes for the life of the session — the child has no reaper and becomes a zombie that outlives its work. THE FIX IS THE SPAWNING SIDE, not the liveness check. A separate defect, already recorded, is that the liveness test reads a zombie as alive because os.kill against a zombie succeeds; that is a real bug and is queued behind another node, but it is a workaround for a corpse that should not exist. Make the launch leave no corpse: reap finished children in the long-lived loop, or double-fork so the child reparents immediately, or install an auto-reap disposition in the process that owns the loop. Choose one, say which and why in your manifest, and do not rely on the caller remembering to reap. FALSIFIERS, all required: a worker launched by an ordinary short-lived dispatch still runs and still survives the parent exiting, since detaching it is the point of start_new_session; a worker launched by the sweep still runs to completion and its stream and manifest are unaffected; after that worker finishes, no defunct child remains under the launching process; and a second resume of the same run is accepted rather than refused. Assert the last two by inspecting process state rather than by asserting the code path was taken. Measure base and head over tests/test_resume_reaps_its_child.py plus every test importing reckon.crew.resumption or reckon.crew.dispatch; report failure ids either side and require none added.
node_definition.goal: Stop a sweep-woken run from leaving a zombie under the long-lived process that woke it, so the next resume of that run is not refused

node_definition.done_when: pytest tests/test_routing_evidence_fields.py -q passes, and a promoted ledger row carries three new fields: the repository paths the node manifest declared under follow_ons, a continuation link naming a predecessor run or absent, and a dispute count or the string unknown. WHY THE EXISTING MEASURE CANNOT ROUTE. Pass rate is saturated at 1.00 across every lane in the committed ledger, because the worker writes its own gate. Rework, defined as a later run touching the earlier node declared write paths in the same project and plan, was the replacement, and it discriminates about four to one, but it counts four different events as one. A node that left a defect which was then repaired is one event. A node that flagged an adjacent problem as a followup, which was then acted on over the same paths, is a second and opposite event scored identically. A node delivering part one of a planned two-part change is a third. A node that disputed the premises of its brief and landed once produces no later touch at all, so that event is invisible. The metric therefore ranks a worker that stays inside its fence above one that reports what it found outside it. THE DISCRIMINATOR EXISTS AND IS NOT ON THE ROW. A worker manifest carries follow_ons naming what it states should happen next, so a later touch of paths the earlier manifest already named is separable from a later touch of paths it did not. The ledger row carries only manifest_path and a free-text outcome, and a run directory can be deleted, so a measure reading the manifest decays as run directories are cleaned. RECORD THREE FIELDS AT PROMOTION, each read from evidence rather than inferred. First, the repository paths named in the promoted node manifest follow_ons. Second, a continuation link naming a predecessor run id, taken from a coordinator-supplied value when present and otherwise from this run base commit matching a predecessor run tip. Third, a count of corrections the worker stated against the factual premises of its brief, read from the worker own report text. DO NOT COMPUTE A NEW RATE IN THIS NODE. It records facts; which measure consumes them is a separate decision and is not this node to make. FALSIFIERS. A promotion whose manifest declares no follow_ons writes an empty list, not a missing key, so a node with nothing to declare is separable from one never measured. A run with no predecessor omits the continuation link rather than writing null. A worker report that parsed and stated no corrections writes 0; a worker report that did not parse writes the string unknown, because 0 and unmeasured are different values and merging them is the failure this node exists to prevent. Every existing ledger field keeps its current value and type, asserted over a row promoted before this change. Measure base and head over tests/test_routing_evidence_fields.py plus every test importing reckon.crew.promotion or reckon.ledger; report failure ids either side and require none added.
node_definition.goal: Record on each promoted row the three facts a routing measure needs, so a later touch can be separated from a defect without reading a file that may be deleted

node_definition.done_when: pytest tests/test_ceiling_holds_regardless_of_burn.py -q passes, and a lane whose utilisation is at or above the ceiling is held whatever the burn floors decide. THE REGRESSION, introduced by commit a7489798 earlier today and live on the primary branch now. That change made burn multiple an admission input behind floors on elapsed fraction and utilisation. Where burn is not admissible it also sets the whole reading's headroom to unknown, and an unknown headroom is never held, by a deliberate and otherwise correct rule that absence of a signal must not be read as exhaustion. The two rules compose into a fail-open. Measured on the current primary branch by constructing the account-surface block that _from_block receives, then asking decide for a dispatch verdict against a 95 percent ceiling. Columns are utilisation, elapsed fraction of the window, resulting headroom, and whether the lane is held. 8 percent at 2.47 percent elapsed gives unknown and not held. 96 percent at 2.47 percent elapsed gives unknown and NOT HELD. 99.5 percent at 2.47 percent elapsed gives unknown and NOT HELD. The same three utilisations at 30 percent elapsed give known, and 96 and 99.5 are held. So a lane with almost none of its quota left is admitted for dispatch whenever the reading is taken early in its window, which is exactly when a burst of dispatches can spend the remainder. Before a7489798 those two rows were held. WHY THE EXISTING SUITE DID NOT CATCH IT. The falsifier written into that node required that each of the nine backends this project configures keep its held or clear verdict. Every one of those nine sits far below the ceiling, so the assertion ranged over a population that could not contain the failure and passed while the regression stood. The suite is green at 120 tests over four files. WHAT TO CHANGE. Separate what the burn floors govern from what they do not. The floors decide whether a projected exhaustion instant is emitted; they must not decide whether utilisation is a known reading. A reading carrying a utilisation figure has known headroom whether or not its burn multiple is admissible, and the ceiling comparison applies to it as it did before. Keep the emitted reason naming both facts, since a reader needs to know the utilisation was used and the projection was withheld. WHAT NOT TO CHANGE. Do not alter the floor values, the projection arithmetic, the degradation to the reset instant at burn at or below one, or the rule that a genuinely absent signal reports unknown and is not held. A reading with no utilisation figure at all still reports unknown. FALSIFIERS, asserted in tests/test_ceiling_holds_regardless_of_burn.py over a RANGE of utilisations rather than over the configured backends, because ranging over the configured backends is the defect that let this through. Across utilisations of 8, 60, 94, 96 and 99.5 percent, and across elapsed fractions both below and above the burn elapsed floor, the held verdict depends on utilisation against the ceiling alone and is identical at both elapsed fractions. A reading at or above the ceiling is held at every elapsed fraction tested. A reading below the ceiling is not held at any of them. A reading whose utilisation is absent reports unknown and is not held, at every elapsed fraction. A projection is still withheld below the floors and still emitted above them, so this changes which facts the floors govern and not the floors. State in the test file docstring that the range is the point, so a later reader does not narrow it back to the configured backends. Measure base and head over tests/test_ceiling_holds_regardless_of_burn.py and every test importing reckon.budget; report failure ids either side and require none added.
node_definition.goal: Restore the utilisation ceiling hold for a lane read early in its window, where the burn floors currently turn a known reading into an unknown one and admit a spent lane

THESE ARE INTEGRATION DRIFT FROM PARALLEL NODES THAT EACH PASSED ALONE; the diagnosis is done and you are repairing rather than investigating. (1) test_the_action_set_is_one_set_with_three_readers and test_every_emitted_state_is_watched_actionable_or_delivered fail because the paused, waiting and wait-aged classifications now live in the classifier own state sets while the ticker action set and the fleet-counter coverage were never updated in step: two nodes landed those states and the monitor surface separately and neither could see the other. The discriminator is already present and observable: on an exhausted run the budget block carries lane_backpressure true and a detail naming the retry count, while on a run that retried and recovered the marker is absent. Join that marker with a dead process so the row names the lane and offers resume. Leave the metered refusal path unchanged. FALSIFIERS, all required: a run that retried and RECOVERED still reads running or complete and is never called blocked, which two runs carrying seven retries each and committing real work demonstrate; a metered usage-limit refusal keeps the reason and reset it has today; a dead run with no retries at all is still abandoned; and the counter buckets still partition every emitted state. THE CORRECTION THIS MAKES. A held commit, reachable as tag held-overdue-wait-placement, reconciled the ticker action set with the fleet counter coverage and in doing so moved the wait-aged state out of the waiting counter and into the blocked counter. It was implemented exactly as its brief instructed and the brief was wrong. Measured: tests/test_external_wait.py::test_an_old_wait_surfaces_its_age_without_becoming_blocked fails on that commit with counts blocked 1 waiting 0 where it asserts blocked 0 waiting 1. THE SEMANTICS TO HOLD, which the existing test already encodes and which the display work exists to serve. A run whose declared external wait has aged past its stall threshold is STILL WAITING on something outside itself. It has not failed, it is not stalled on anything a reader can clear by inspecting it, and reporting it in the blocked count produces the alarming signal that this display work was undertaken to remove. What is true of it is that its condition has not lifted when expected, and that fact belongs in the ACTION MARKER a reader sees on the row, not in the blocked tally. So the two facts are carried by two different mechanisms and must not be collapsed into one: the COUNT says what kind of thing this run is, and the MARKER says whether a reader should look at it. WHAT TO DO. Take the held commit as the starting point rather than reimplementing it: git show held-overdue-wait-placement gives its full diff, and the parts reconciling the action set with the counter coverage are wanted. Keep every part that places paused and waiting in the progress family. Do not modify tests/test_external_wait.py; it states the contract this node exists to honour, and amending it would be the node marking its own homework. WHAT NOT TO CHANGE. The action set and the counter coverage agree on every state, which is what the held commit set out to achieve and what must survive. A paused run and a waiting run are both counted in the waiting family and neither carries the action marker. node_definition.done_when: pytest tests/test_follow_sweep_cadence.py -q passes, and the recovery sweep runs on its declared cadence while a follower is attached to a live producer stream. THE MEASUREMENT. reckon/crew/resumption.py declares DEFAULT_SWEEP_SECONDS 120.0, described in its own comment as short enough that a lane returning minutes later is picked up while the wave still matters. The status file at the recovery directory records swept_at 2026-09-06T15:08:27Z and swept_by_pid 4176213. That pid is a live crew follow process for this project, the producer is live, and four worker transitions were emitted to its pane at 15:18Z, 15:23Z, 15:38Z and 16:11Z. At 16:17Z the recorded sweep was 69 minutes old against a 120 second cadence. A second project reports the same shape: a run whose declared wait had been satisfied sat eligible for roughly 35 minutes with a live follower and no wake, and resume-ready run by hand picked it up at once. THE MECHANISM, in the follow loop in reckon/cli.py. The cadence gate is called at the top of the outer loop, once per outer iteration. The loop then opens the producer stream and enters an inner while True that reads lines, ticks, and sleeps. That inner loop never calls the cadence gate. It exits only when the follower is stopped or the producer stops being live. So while a producer stays up, the outer loop never iterates again and the sweep runs exactly once, at attach. The 120 second cadence is therefore not a cadence at all; it is a lower bound that only takes effect after a producer dies and the follower reattaches. A busy fleet and a quiet fleet are equally affected, because the inner loop is entered either way. WHAT TO CHANGE. The sweep must run on elapsed time while the follower is inside the stream read loop. Call the cadence gate from the inner loop on the same passes that already tick and sleep, so a follower reading a live stream sweeps on its declared interval. Keep the gate itself unchanged: it is already time since last sweep rather than a count of iterations, and it already guards against a tight poll becoming a hot path. Do not raise or lower DEFAULT_SWEEP_SECONDS, do not change what sweep does, and do not change the pane output; a sweep writes to the status file and the recovery log, and nothing about the follower belongs on the transition stream. WHY THIS IS NOT MERELY A MISSED WAKE. The sweep is what turns a parked run back into a running one, so a follower that stops sweeping converts every declared external wait into a manual operation while continuing to display as a healthy attached follower. The status file exists precisely because a sweep that ran and found nothing and a sweep that never ran are otherwise indistinguishable; that file is what made this measurable, and its stamp is the evidence above. FALSIFIERS, each asserted in tests/test_follow_sweep_cadence.py with an injected clock and an injected sweep so no real follower and no real provider are involved. A follower attached to a live producer stream that emits no lines for several cadence intervals calls the sweep once per interval, not once in total. A follower reading a stream that emits lines continuously calls the sweep on the cadence, so line traffic neither starves the sweep nor multiplies it. Two calls inside one interval produce one sweep, so the existing rate guard still holds from the inner loop. A sweep that raises does not end the follower and does not stop later sweeps. A stopped follower performs no sweep after it is stopped. The pane output for a given sequence of stream lines is byte-identical to the output before this change, asserted by comparing emitted lines with the sweep injected as a no-op. Measure base and head over tests/test_follow_sweep_cadence.py and every test importing reckon.cli or reckon.crew.resumption; report failure ids either side and require none added.
node_definition.goal: Make the follower's recovery sweep run on its declared interval while it is reading a live producer stream, instead of once at attach

node_definition.done_when: pytest tests/test_a_served_turn_refutes_the_refusal.py -q passes, and a refusal in a run's stream stops holding that run once the same stream shows the lane served a turn after it. THE MEASUREMENT, from a peer project across one afternoon. A run parked when a metered window closed at 14:07Z carried a refusal naming a reset two days out. The lane then served six turns under that same run, and the hold stood through every one of them; a person resumed the run by hand four times, and roughly eighteen hand resumes were needed across the fleet that afternoon. The hold text asserts that a served turn on the backend refreshes this evidence. Nothing in reckon/budget.py keys on served turns, so that sentence describes a mechanism that was never built, which is worse than silence because a reader waits for something that cannot happen. THE MECHANISM. _refusal_event_stamp walks a run's stream, finds the NEWEST rate_limit_event whose status is rejected, and dates it from the nearest surrounding timestamped record. DEFAULT_SHELF_LIFE_MINUTES then ages a refusal that names NO reset. A refusal that names a reset is exempt from that ageing and is trusted until the named instant. The comment beside the shelf life already records why a hold cannot clear itself: only a served run writes a budget record, and the hold refuses every run, so the lane is unreachable by the one thing that would update it. That reasoning applies identically to a dated refusal and was not applied to it, because a provider's stated reset was treated as authoritative. The measurement above refutes that assumption, and an earlier incident on this workstation recorded a stated reset clause wrong by three and a half hours, so it is not one provider's slip. WHY THE FIX IS CHEAP. The refutation is already parsed. That function loads the whole stream and already locates the newest rejected event by index. It never asks whether anything after that index succeeded. WHAT TO CHANGE. After locating the newest rejected event, determine from the SAME parsed events whether the lane served a turn at a later stream position. If it did, that refusal no longer describes now, and the run is not held on it. Choose the marker of a served turn from what the stream actually carries and state in a comment which record shape you chose and why; a retry that was itself rejected is not a served turn, and neither is a record that merely mentions a rejection. Where no later served turn exists, behaviour is unchanged. WHAT NOT TO CHANGE. Do not alter the shelf life, the floors, the projected exhaustion path, the ceiling comparison, or the treatment of a refusal that names no reset. Do not weaken a refusal that names a future reset and has no served turn after it; that evidence is current and holding on it is this module's purpose. Do not read any file other than the stream already being read. FALSIFIERS, asserted in tests/test_a_served_turn_refutes_the_refusal.py against constructed streams rather than a live account. A stream whose newest rejected event is followed by a served turn does not hold the run, and the emitted reason names the served turn as what refuted it. A stream whose newest rejected event is followed by nothing still holds, unchanged. A stream whose newest rejected event is followed only by further rejected events still holds, so a retry storm does not read as recovery. A refusal naming a future reset with no later served turn still holds, and its reason is unchanged. A refusal naming a reset already past does not hold, unchanged. A stream carrying the rejection phrase only inside an assistant or user record, which is how a worker discussing rate limits or reading a test fixture appears, is not treated as a rejection at all: measured across two fleets on 2026-09-06, 98,000 records carried 516 such substring hits and zero genuine rejections, so a phrase-matching implementation would hold every run that talks about rate limiting. Measure base and head over the new file and every test importing reckon.budget; report failure ids either side and require none added.
node_definition.goal: Stop holding a run on a refusal its own stream shows was overtaken by a served turn

node_definition.done_when: pytest tests/test_sweep_status_is_per_writer.py -q passes, and a reader can establish when a NAMED follower last swept, separately from every other writer of that project's sweep record. WHY THIS EXISTS. The sweep status file carries one slot per project, holding swept_at and swept_by_pid for whichever writer wrote last. Its own comment states the purpose it was built for: a sweep that ran and found nothing and a sweep that never ran are otherwise indistinguishable. It achieves that for the project. It cannot answer the question a reader actually asks, which is whether THEIR follower is sweeping. MEASURED 2026-09-06, across two projects. On one, a stamp read at 16:17Z showed a pid and a time 69 minutes old, and was used as evidence that a specific follower had stopped sweeping; the file is written by every follower on the project, by availability probes, and by hand-run sweeps from the command line and from the MCP surface, so the stamp was only the last write by any writer. On the second project a reader found a stamp written by a HAND-RUN sweep and would have taken it for follower cadence had its author not recognised the pid. Two followers were then observed alternating in one file, 120 seconds apart each, so neither one's cadence could be read from it. A wrong conclusion was published to two sessions on the strength of that file and had to be retracted. WHAT TO CHANGE. Record one entry per writer rather than one per project, keyed so that a reader can ask for a specific writer and get that writer's last sweep. Carry on each entry what the writer was: a follower sweeping on its cadence, a hand-run sweep from the command line or the MCP surface, or any other caller, since a reader distinguishing follower health from their own manual pass needs that distinction and cannot infer it from a pid. Keep a project-level view for the existing readers so nothing that reads the current shape loses its answer. Bound the file: a writer that no longer exists must not accumulate forever, and state in a comment which bound you chose and why. WHAT NOT TO CHANGE. Do not alter the cadence, what a sweep does, when it runs, or the append-only recovery log beside it. Do not make a reader's question require a process lookup: the record must answer from its own contents, because a pid on a shared filesystem is meaningless on another host, and this project's crew home is shared across login nodes. FALSIFIERS, asserted in tests/test_sweep_status_is_per_writer.py against a temporary configuration directory, with an assertion that the real configuration directory gains no file. Two writers writing in sequence both remain readable afterwards, and neither entry is overwritten by the other. A reader asking for one writer gets that writer's last sweep and not another's. A reader asking for a writer that never wrote gets an answer meaning unknown, distinguishable from an answer meaning that writer swept and found nothing. A hand-run sweep and a follower cadence sweep are distinguishable in the record without consulting any process. The project-level view still answers what it answers today for a single-writer file. The bound removes entries by its stated rule and by nothing else, asserted by writing past the bound and checking which entries survive. Measure base and head over the new file and every test importing reckon.crew.resumption; report failure ids either side and require none added.
node_definition.goal: Let a reader establish when their own follower last swept, separately from probes, hand-run sweeps and other followers writing the same project record

node_definition.done_when: pytest tests/test_a_zombie_is_not_alive.py -q passes, and a pid in the kernel's zombie state reports as not alive. THE MEASUREMENT, reported by a peer session and cross-session in a way that matters. A resume launched by one session's project-wide recovery sweep resumed another session's run. When the resumed process ended, its child remained as a defunct entry under the SPAWNING session's follower pid for about three hours. During that window reckon refused the owning session's own resume attempt with the reason that the run still has a live process, because os.kill against a zombie succeeds. The owning session could not clear it: the parent was another session's follower, so the only party able to reap it was the party that did not know it was holding anything. THE MECHANISM, in reckon/crew/runs.py. process_alive signals the pid with a zero signal and reports the outcome. A zombie is a process table entry whose process has exited and whose exit status has not been collected; the kernel accepts a zero signal against it, so this function returns True. Its docstring reasons carefully about a PermissionError meaning the process belongs to another user and is therefore proof of life; it does not reason about the state the process is in. THE SIGNAL IS ALREADY BEING READ IN THIS FILE. _process_start_time, the function immediately below, opens the per-process stat record under /proc for that pid and parses it for the start tick that distinguishes reused process ids. The process state is a field on that same line. So the file already reads the record that answers this and uses one field from it. WHY REAPING IS NOT THE WHOLE ANSWER, so this node is not made redundant by the reaper. Launched workers are registered with a reaper that collects them on a background thread, so a zombie is expected to be short-lived. Reaping is asynchronous, which means there is always a window in which the process has exited and its status has not been collected, and during that window every reader of this function gets the wrong answer in the dangerous direction: a finished run reported as running holds its slot, refuses its own resume, and cannot be cleared by whoever owns it. A window that is usually brief is still a window, and the peer measured one lasting three hours. WHAT TO CHANGE. A pid whose kernel state is zombie reports as not alive. Read the state from the same per-process stat record this file already parses. Where that record cannot be read at all, behaviour is unchanged, because an unreadable record is not proof of death and this module already declines to treat unprovable liveness as death. Say in a comment why a zombie is not alive for this function's purpose: its process has exited, so every caller asking whether work is still running wants no. WHAT NOT TO CHANGE. Do not alter the PermissionError branch, which correctly reports a process owned by another user as alive. Do not alter the branch returning None when there is no pid or the pid is not an integer. Do not change the reaper, its registration, or its thread. Do not read any file for a pid other than the one asked about. FALSIFIERS, asserted in tests/test_a_zombie_is_not_alive.py. A pid whose per-process stat record reports the zombie state returns not alive. A pid whose record reports a running, sleeping, stopped or uninterruptible-sleep state returns alive, asserted across each of those states rather than only one, so the change narrows to the zombie case alone. A pid with no per-process stat record at all returns as it does today. A pid whose per-process stat record exists and cannot be parsed returns as it does today rather than raising. A pid of None or a non-integer returns as it does today. A real spawned child that has exited and not been waited on reports not alive, and the same child reports alive before it exits, asserted against an actual process rather than a constructed record, so the field offset being read is proven against the kernel rather than against a fixture. Measure base and head over the new file and every test importing reckon.crew.runs; report failure ids either side and require none added, noting that the dispatch-arming and watcher-lifetime failures in that set are environmental and equal on both sides.

node_definition.done_when: pytest tests/test_a_reexec_keeps_its_children.py -q passes, and a follower that replaces its own process image still collects the workers it launched before the replacement. THE MEASUREMENT, cross-session and confirmed on both sides. One session's project-wide recovery sweep resumed another session's run at about 21:24Z. The spawned child ended and remained defunct under the spawning follower's pid for roughly three hours, until that follower was replaced at 00:44Z. Throughout the window reckon refused the OWNING session's resume with the reason that the run still has a live process, because a zero signal against a defunct entry succeeds. The owning session could not clear it, because the parent was another session's follower. The follower's pid was 2466472, started 18:12:32Z, which is 87 minutes AFTER the reaper landed, so it was running code that registers every launched pid with a reaper thread and it still did not collect the child. THE MECHANISM, and it is why the reaper was present and ineffective. The follower checks at a bounded cadence whether it should adopt newly installed code and replaces its own process image with os.execv in reckon/cli.py. A process image replacement keeps the pid and keeps the parent-child relationships, and destroys every thread and all module state. So after a replacement the reaper thread no longer exists, the set of launched pids is empty, and the process remains the parent of children it can no longer name. Those children can never be collected by anyone: their parent is alive, so they are not reparented to the init process that would collect them, and their parent has forgotten them. The reaper is not broken; it is discarded along with the registry that told it what to wait for. A SECOND DEFECT IN THE SAME AREA, which the falsifiers must cover because it produces the same symptom by a different route. The helper that starts the reaper returns early when a thread object is already recorded, and never asks whether that thread is still running. A thread that has ended for any reason leaves its object in place, so every later launch takes the early return and the reaper is never started again for the life of the process, with nothing reporting it. WHAT TO CHANGE. Carry the outstanding launched pids across the process image replacement so the new image continues to own them and collects them as they end. The replacement path already has a preparation step where a reader checkpoint is written, which is where the handover belongs. Choose the carrier so that it survives an image replacement and state in a comment why the others were rejected. The new image adopts what it is handed and registers those pids exactly as if it had launched them, because it is the same process and it is still their parent. Separately, the helper that starts the reaper starts one whenever no live reaper is running rather than whenever no thread object is recorded. WHAT NOT TO CHANGE. Do not delay or block the image replacement waiting for children to finish; a follower that stops adopting new code to wait on a worker is a worse failure than the one being fixed. Do not change what the reaper does with a pid it owns. Do not reap a child a caller manages synchronously; the existing rule that only registered launch pids are touched must hold across the handover. Do not change the cadence at which the replacement is considered. FALSIFIERS, asserted in tests/test_a_reexec_keeps_its_children.py. Pids outstanding at the moment of a replacement appear in the new image's registry, asserted on the registry rather than on the carrier. A pid registered before a replacement and exiting after it is collected, asserted against a real spawned child rather than a constructed record. A replacement with no outstanding pids hands over nothing and the new image starts clean. A carrier that is absent, empty or unparseable leaves the new image with an empty registry and does not raise, because a follower that refuses to start is worse than one that misses a reap. The reaper starter starts a new reaper when the recorded thread has ended, and does not start a second one when the recorded thread is running, asserted by counting live reaper threads across repeated calls. A caller-managed child is still never collected by the reaper after a handover. Measure base and head over the new file and every test importing reckon.crew.dispatch or reckon.cli; report failure ids either side and require none added, noting that the dispatch-arming and watcher-lifetime failures in that set are environmental and equal on both sides.

node_definition.done_when: pytest tests/test_manifest_log_paths_are_durable.py -q passes, and a promoted run whose manifest cites a test log under the shared temporary directory is reported rather than recorded silently. THE MEASUREMENT, from this session's own promotions. Three separate workers wrote their test logs under the shared temporary directory despite the dispatch contract naming the run directory: their manifests cite paths beginning with the temporary root, and the coordinator noticed only while reading the manifests by hand. Two of the three were this coordinator's own nodes. WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND TIDINESS. Those logs are the evidence a promotion cites. A promoted ledger row names a gate command, an exit status and a log path, and the log path is what a later reader opens to check the claim. The shared temporary directory on this workstation is a small allocation that is cleared without notice, so a promotion can carry a citation to a file that no longer exists, and nothing distinguishes that from a citation to a file that was never written. The run directory persists with the run; the temporary root does not. WHAT TO CHANGE. Add a check over a manifest's cited log paths that reports any path resolving under the shared temporary root, naming the manifest, the key and the offending path. It reports; it does not refuse, rewrite or relocate anything. A path under the run directory, under the repository, or under any other durable location is not reported. The temporary root is what the standard library reports as the platform temporary directory, read from the running system rather than written as a literal, and a path is under it when its resolved form is contained by that resolved root, so a symlinked or relative spelling is caught rather than only a literal prefix. WHAT NOT TO CHANGE. Do not alter promotion, the gate requirement, the ledger row, or any classification. Do not refuse a promotion on this finding: a coordinator promoting a run whose logs are already written cannot make them durable, and refusing would strand the record rather than improve it. Do not touch the manifest file. Do not check any path other than those a manifest cites as logs. A manifest citing a log under the repository is not reported. A manifest citing no logs is not reported and does not raise. A manifest whose cited path does not exist on disk is judged by where it points rather than by whether it exists, because a missing durable path and a missing temporary path are different findings. A path that reaches the temporary root through a symbolic link or a relative spelling is reported, asserted by constructing such a path rather than by asserting on a prefix string. THE MEASUREMENT, reported by a peer project. Five edit_plan calls in one evening were rejected with a validation error stating that ops should be a valid list, with input_type str and the input value shown as the serialised ops text. Structurally identical calls minutes apart succeeded. So the correlation is with payload shape rather than with any one character, and the peer's reading is that the client hands the argument through as JSON text for some payloads. The consequence is that plan state cannot be written through that channel for long bodies; the peer preserved the record by writing it into the cumulative evidence document instead, so nothing was lost, but the comment channel was unreliable for an evening. WHERE TO FIX IT. reckon/mcp.py wraps each strict tool's argument model in a subclass carrying a before-mode validator that rejects unknown parameter names. That validator sees the raw incoming mapping before any field is coerced, and is the point where a serialised list can be recognised. WHAT TO CHANGE. When an argument declared as a list arrives as text that parses as JSON to a list, use the parsed list. Apply it to every argument the model declares as a list rather than to one named argument, because the variance is in how a client serialises and not in which tool is being called. Leave every other case to the existing validation so a genuine type error still reports as one. WHAT NOT TO CHANGE. Do not alter the rejection of unknown parameter names, which is what that validator exists for. Do not coerce an argument the model declares as text, even when its content parses as JSON: an authored HTML argument can legitimately contain bracketed text, and rewriting it would corrupt a document rather than reject a call. Do not accept text that parses to something other than a list for a list argument. Do not accept text that does not parse. Do not change any tool's declared schema, so a client reading the schema still sees a list. FALSIFIERS, asserted in tests/test_tool_arguments_accept_a_serialised_list.py. A list argument delivered as JSON text produces the same result as the same argument delivered as a list, asserted by comparing the two outcomes rather than by asserting the call merely succeeded. A list argument delivered as JSON text that parses to a mapping is rejected, and the message names the argument. A list argument delivered as text that does not parse is rejected, and the message names the argument. A list argument delivered as an integer is rejected as it is today. AN ARGUMENT DECLARED AS TEXT WHOSE VALUE PARSES AS A JSON LIST IS PASSED THROUGH UNCHANGED, asserted on an authored HTML argument containing a bracketed list, because coercing it would corrupt a document. An unknown parameter name is still rejected with the existing message listing the accepted names. A tool's published schema still declares the argument as a list. Measure base and head over the new file and every test importing reckon.mcp; report failure ids either side and require none added. node_definition.done_when: pytest tests/test_figure_index_covers_animations.py -q passes, and a GIF under a project's figures directory appears in the Figures index with its real pixel dimensions, and adding one invalidates the discovery cache. THE MEASUREMENT, reported by a peer project and confirmed here by reading and running the code. A consuming project holds 48 GIFs against 437 PNG and SVG files, and every GIF is absent from the index while remaining fetchable by URL, so it is reachable and invisible. FOUR CALL SITES, each verified rather than taken on report. First, figure_rows in reckon/figures.py builds its inventory from two globs, one for png and one for svg, so a GIF produces no row. Second, the same function chooses a dimension reader with a two-way expression that reads the png reader when the suffix is png and the svg reader otherwise. A GIF therefore takes the svg branch, which reads a binary file as text with replacement and fails its regex, returning nothing. Confirmed by running that reader against a constructed GIF: it returns None while the file's own header states 640 by 480. That is a wrong answer rather than a loud one, which is why nobody saw it. Third, _discovery_signature in reckon/serve.py globs the same two extensions, so a newly written GIF does not change the signature. This one matters on its own: fixing the index without fixing the signature would look correct until somebody added a figure to a running server, at which point the index would not refresh. Fourth, the figure_rows docstring states one row per PNG or SVG. WHAT TO CHANGE. Include GIFs wherever those two extensions are gathered, in both files. Make the dimension dispatch three-way rather than two-way, so each format reaches a reader written for it and no format falls through to another's. Read a GIF's dimensions from its own header with no new dependency: the first six bytes are the signature GIF87a or GIF89a, and bytes six through nine are the logical screen width and height as little-endian unsigned shorts, so the reader checks the signature and unpacks those four bytes, in the same shape as the existing png reader. Update the docstring with the rest. WHAT NEEDS NO CHANGE, verified so the node does not widen: figures are served through the standard library's type guesser, which already reports image/gif, and the gallery thumbnail is a plain image element, which animates a GIF natively, so no frame extraction and no imaging dependency are required. WHAT NOT TO CHANGE. Do not alter how titles or captions are resolved; that path reads a sidecar and is already format-agnostic. Do not alter the row shape, the ordering key, or the project segmentation. Do not add a dependency. Do not change what is served or how. Do not make an unreadable or truncated GIF raise: a file whose signature is absent or whose header is short reports no dimensions, exactly as a malformed PNG does today, because a figures index that refuses to render because one file is corrupt is worse than one row without dimensions. FALSIFIERS, asserted in tests/test_figure_index_covers_animations.py against a temporary figures tree the test creates. A GIF produces an inventory row, and that row carries the width and height from its header, asserted on a file whose dimensions are not square so a transposed unpack is caught. Both signature forms, GIF87a and GIF89a, are read. A PNG's dimensions and an SVG's dimensions are unchanged from what they are today, asserted on the same fixtures in the same test run so a three-way dispatch cannot have altered either. A GIF whose signature bytes are wrong yields a row with no dimensions and does not raise. A GIF truncated inside its header yields a row with no dimensions and does not raise. The discovery signature changes when a GIF is added to the tree and is stable when nothing changes, asserted by taking the signature twice around the addition rather than by inspecting the glob. Row count for a tree of one PNG, one SVG and one GIF is three. Measure base and head over the new file plus every test importing reckon.figures or exercising the discovery signature; report failure ids either side and require none added. WHY IT IS DERIVED IN PYTHON RATHER THAN DECIDED IN THE SURFACE. This repository's binding rule is that the surface renders and does not derive, and its test is one question: would an agent, a CLI caller or an MCP read have any use for this value. All three want to know the fetchable file for an artifact, so it is a fact and belongs on the row. The alternative the rule forbids is a conditional in the reader keyed on the kind, which puts the kind enumeration in two places and lets the two surfaces disagree later. There is no boolean beside it, deliberately: a boolean beside an href is a second source of truth for one fact, and a field cannot disagree with itself. The reader then needs one kind-agnostic line, that an empty download disables the control. WHAT TO CHANGE. figure_rows in reckon/figures.py emits rows of two kinds, figure and gif. SCOPE IT TO THIS PRODUCER. Do not add the field to rows produced anywhere else, and do not chase the document kinds. The lead has explicitly deferred document download, and an absent field is falsy, so a reader disables the control for those rows today with no further work; when document download is authorised, that producer adds the same field and the reader lights up unchanged. node_definition.done_when: pytest tests/test_follow_observes_other_sessions.py -q passes, and one follower delivers transitions for its own session plus any number of named other sessions, registering delivery for its own session alone. WHAT THE LEAD ASKED FOR, in their words: extend the monitor to enable an attach to multiple sessions, because it is useful when tracking old work in addition to our own, and they suggested an appended session. WHY THE OBVIOUS IMPLEMENTATION IS UNSAFE, and this is the constraint the node exists to honour. The follow command's session option does two things, not one: it narrows delivery to the runs that session dispatched, AND it registers the session as attached. Dispatch refuses a session whose runs would finish unheard, and that refusal is decided on the attachment record. So a follower that registered attachment for a second session would satisfy the OTHER coordinator's dispatch precondition with delivery that ends when this session ends. Their guard would read as cleared while the thing it guards against became true, which is the failure this fleet has spent a night removing: a guard satisfied by evidence that does not mean what it claims. WHAT TO CHANGE. Keep the existing session option exactly as it is: one value, the owning session, narrowing delivery and registering attachment. Add a separate repeatable option naming other sessions to observe. Transitions for an observed session are delivered to the pane. Nothing is registered for an observed session: no attachment record, no delivery claim, no effect on any dispatch guard anywhere. Say in the option's help text that observing does not vouch for delivery, so a reader of the command line knows which half they are getting. A row from an observed session is marked as another session's, and the ticker already carries a marker for exactly that meaning; use it rather than inventing a second spelling. WHAT NOT TO CHANGE. Do not alter what the existing session option does, its name, or its registration. Do not alter the producer seat, its arming, or the watcher record. Do not alter which transitions are emitted for the owning session. Do not add a way to observe every session at once: the lead asked to name old work alongside their own, and an all-sessions mode would deliver another fleet's whole history into a pane sized for one coordinator's attention. Do not change the ticker's column widths or its marker's spelling; if the marker turns out to need a change, block and say so rather than reaching outside the fence. FALSIFIERS, asserted in tests/test_follow_observes_other_sessions.py against constructed pointers and a temporary configuration home, with an assertion that the real configuration home gains no file. A follower given an owning session and two observed sessions delivers transitions for all three. The attachment record names the owning session only, asserted by reading the record rather than by reading the command's output. A dispatch guard consulted for an observed session reports no delivery, asserted through whatever the guard reads rather than by asserting on the follower. A follower given no observed sessions behaves exactly as it does today, asserted against the same expected lines as the existing single-session case. Rows from an observed session carry the other-session marker and rows from the owning session do not. An observed session named identically to the owning session does not produce duplicate rows for one transition. An observed session that dispatched nothing yields no rows and no error. Naming an observed session does not change what any other session's dispatch is permitted to do, asserted by checking the guard for a third session that was neither owned nor observed. Measure base and head over the new file plus every test importing reckon.cli or reckon.crew.runs; report failure ids either side and require none added, and bound the run per file rather than issuing one census, because that set contains a test which does not complete in this environment.
