node_definition.done_when: The document docs/research/deploy-matrix.html carries the topology measurements below, each with its observation date and its derivation, and no figure is presented in a form that invites the misreading its source warns about. Then: grep for the string 2.44 and for the string 1.12 in that file and confirm neither appears adjacent to the words concurrent workers, and grep for 30% and confirm the prefix-cache figure is not stated as thirty percent anywhere. WHAT ARRIVED, from the session that owns the deployment, measured today from each engine's own startup report. Per topology at a max model length of 1,048,576: the four-card topology reports a KV pool between 2,554,833 and 2,557,835 tokens with a kv_cache_max_concurrency of 2.44; the two-card topology reports 1,173,125 tokens with 1.12. Per-request decode is 23.3 tokens per second on four cards and 23.1 on two. Prefix cache is 17.0 percent cumulative over the four-card window. THE TWO CAVEATS ARE THE POINT, NOT FOOTNOTES. First, kv_cache_max_concurrency counts requests at the maximum context length, not sessions. At the roughly 83,000 tokens an agentic worker actually holds, four cards fit about thirty concurrent and two cards about fourteen. A matrix that recorded 2.44 as two concurrent workers would understate capacity by an order of magnitude, and that is the specific misreading the measuring session asked to have prevented. Record the raw figure, record what it counts, and record the derived figure at realistic context beside it with the 83,000 stated as the assumption it is. Second, the four-card pool differed by about 3,000 tokens between two launches of the SAME profile, so it is approximate and must not be written as a constant to assert against; state the range and the fact that it moved between launches. THE ROW THE MEASURING SESSION MOST WANTS CARRIED: per-request decode is unchanged between the two topologies, 23.3 against 23.1. Cards buy pool and long-context headroom, not speed. State it as the finding it is, because it is the row people assume the other way. A ZERO-DOWNTIME ROTATION IS NOW DEMONSTRATED RATHER THAN REASONED. Four cards to two to four across one day; the second rotation had no dark window because the new topology came up on its own port while the old kept serving, the router preferred it on card count, and only then did the old one stop. Record that traffic moves on health rather than on a timer, so an engine that never becomes reachable leaves the old one serving. Record that this rests on two properties first exercised with two real serves up today: the router collapsing a duplicate model identifier onto the widest topology, which previously returned a conflict on every request, and the endpoint document republishing on both serve and shutdown, which tracked a port moving 18800 to 18809 to 18800 across two rotations with no operator step. A DEFECT THAT DESERVES ITS OWN ROW BECAUSE IT IS NOT ABOUT CAPACITY. A consuming project had its client address pinned to a serve port and was unable to run for hours during the two-card window while the model served normally, because its gate treats an unreachable compose endpoint as fatal to the entire run, so unrelated pools refused to start. The cause was documentation naming a serve port under a heading about what to point a client at. The rule to record: only the router address is stable; a serve port belongs to a profile at a topology and rotates. WHAT TO CORRECT. If the document carries a prefix-cache figure near thirty percent, replace it with 17.0 percent cumulative and state the window, because the earlier figure was generalised from three early spot readings on a warm working set and the cumulative figure is roughly half. WHAT NOT TO CHANGE. Do not alter any existing measured cell, its date or its derivation. Do not convert a cell marked unmeasured into a measured one unless this message supplies the measurement. Do not restate the ledger filters in section eight. Do not add a lane, remove a lane, or change the row-per-backend shape. Do not present any capacity figure as a ceiling: this document's own discipline is that a lane ceiling belongs to its deployment and is discovered rather than assumed, and these figures are capacity reports from a startup log, not probed limits. FALSIFIERS. Every figure added carries its observation date and how it was obtained. The raw concurrency figures appear only beside a statement of what they count. The derived thirty and fourteen appear only beside the 83,000-token assumption they rest on. The pool figure appears as a range with the between-launch variation stated. No sentence claims cards increase per-request speed. The rotation account names health rather than elapsed time as what moves traffic. The address rule names the router as the only stable address. Any prefix-cache figure in the document reads 17.0 percent with its window. The document still parses as the reckon research type it declares, with its existing meta unchanged.

node_definition.done_when: grep for the phrase durable write in skills/reckon-ship/references/worker-protocol.md and confirm the file states that a worker commits at each deliverable and writes its manifest before beginning any long output or any wait, with the measured reason beside it; then confirm the file still contains its existing manifest-path and delivery sections unchanged by diffing those sections against the previous revision. THE MEASUREMENT, compiled across two fleets on one locally served lane and reported independently by three sessions. Forty runs. On the reporting fleets, small-scope code-changing nodes with a named check landed and scored 9 or 10 out of 10 in independent review, while broad-reading and report-shaped nodes died late with a response that stopped arriving or a request that timed out. One fleet: implement 8 of 8 passed, conformance reviews 7 of 7, investigate scouts 0 of 5. The other: code-changing nodes 5 of 6, report-shaped nodes 3 of 8. THE MECHANISM, AND TWO EARLIER EXPLANATIONS WERE WITHDRAWN BEFORE THIS ONE. A tokens-per-second discriminator held on 14 runs and did not reproduce on 26, where passes ran 1.69 to 6.54 output tokens per second and failures 1.79 to 6.12, so the reporting session retracted it and recommends no rate-based abort rule. A context-accumulation explanation was also withdrawn and inverted by the larger sample: per-turn context was HIGHER in the survivors, 107,000 to 215,000 input tokens per turn against 41,000 to 101,000 in the dead scouts, and the largest run of all passed at 173 turns and 37.1 million cumulative input tokens. Turn count and cumulative input separate nothing. What survives both samples is narrower: the failure is a long single output late in a long session under load. Neither fleet lost a node whose brief made the deliverable a small, early, incremental write. Two partial survivors are the evidence: one wrote its findings into its manifest and then died before its report, so the findings survived; another committed and then died, so the commit survived. Both survived because the durable write came before the long output. Four total losses each had the report as one final generation. WHY THE LANE MAKES THIS WORSE RATHER THAN CAUSING IT. Every stream in both fleets carries a prompt-cache read of zero and a cache creation of zero, so context is re-sent in full every turn; the heaviest node re-sent 37.1 million input tokens across 173 turns. A broad brief on this lane is therefore not merely slower, it is self-terminating. WHAT TO ADD TO THE FILE. State that a worker commits at each deliverable rather than once at the end, and writes its manifest before beginning any long output and before any wait. State the reason as measured rather than as advice: a durable write that precedes the long generation survives the generation failing, and every total loss in forty runs had its deliverable as one final output. State that this is why a node whose deliverable is a report should write that report incrementally to its file as it is produced, rather than composing it in one closing generation. Keep the existing rule that long output goes in the file and the reply is the path, and connect the new text to it rather than restating it. WHAT NOT TO CHANGE. Do not alter the eight node properties or their order. Do not alter the manifest-path section, the delivery section, or the fence descriptions. Do not add a rate-based abort rule, a turn-count limit, or a context-size limit: all three were measured and none discriminates, and the file must not acquire a threshold the data refutes. Do not name a backend, a model or a lane: the property is about where the durable write falls relative to the long output, and a file naming this lane would read as inapplicable on another. Do not state a figure for how long a generation may take. FALSIFIERS. The file states the commit-at-each-deliverable rule and the manifest-before-long-output rule. Each carries its measured reason rather than an assertion. The words tokens per second, turn limit and context limit do not appear as a rule anywhere in the file. No backend or model name appears in the added text. The existing manifest-path and delivery sections are byte-identical to the previous revision, asserted by diffing them. The added text refers to the existing long-output-goes-in-the-file rule rather than duplicating it. The file's front matter and section numbering are unchanged.

node_definition.done_when: The document docs/research/deploy-matrix.html states that the glm lane is withdrawn with its date and reason, carries the effort-versus-durable-cost figures below, and carries the spark profile below; then grep the file and confirm the glm rows are marked withdrawn rather than deleted, and confirm no sentence recommends a lower effort for any node class. THREE CHANGES, ALL MEASURED, ALL DATED 2026-09-08. FIRST, THE GLM LANE IS WITHDRAWN. The lead has dropped it: the model does not fit the serving deployment alongside capacity for other work. Mark the lane withdrawn with that reason and date. Do not delete its cells and do not scrub its rows from the matrix, because a withdrawn lane that was measured is a record and a reader comparing lanes later needs to know it existed and why it went. State alongside it that the lane was never cleanly measured: nine rows, zero passing, and the classifications were six malformed-node and three infrastructure-failure, so two thirds were coordinator brief defects and the remaining three trace to a window defect on that lane. The honest cell is not that the model performed poorly; it is that no clean measurement of it exists. SECOND, EFFORT DOES NOT WANT A DISPATCH KNOB, AND THE MEDIAN HIDES WHY. Measured on the committed ledger over the sol model, which carries the only two-effort sample large enough to compare: at high effort 266 runs, 246 durable, 92 percent, median wall 568 seconds, total wall 38.2 hours, and 558 seconds of wall per durable node. At medium effort 236 runs, 207 durable, 88 percent, median wall 492 seconds, total wall 48.6 hours, and 846 seconds of wall per durable node. So medium is faster per run by median and 52 percent dearer per durable node, and it consumed more total wall while producing fewer durable nodes. State the median beside the per-durable figure precisely because the median inverts the conclusion, and a reader who sees only the median will route to the wrong effort. The finding to record is that effort trades turns rather than buying quality, and the unit-of-work cost favours a uniform high effort over a routing knob. WHAT MUST NOT BE OVERSTATED IN THAT CELL. Generated tokens per durable node run the other way, 6.9 thousand at high against 3.6 thousand at medium, and generation is not what a subscription meter charges. Cumulative input per run is not recorded anywhere in the ledger, only a peak, so the exact quota cost per durable node is unmeasured and must be marked so. Record the wall-per-durable figure as the strongest available evidence and record the quota-cost figure as absent rather than inferring it from wall. THIRD, THE SPARK PROFILE, WHICH IS NARROW AND CONSISTENT. Nine rows, every one role implement at spec level exact, eight durable, median wall 236 seconds, 249 seconds of wall per durable node. That is 2.2 times cheaper per durable node than sol at high effort, on the one node shape it has been given. State that the sample is nine and that it spans a single role and a single spec level, so it supports a hypothesis about focused well-specified implementation work and supports nothing about any other shape. State that spark carries its own separate quota window rather than sharing the primary one, which is why it is worth measuring rather than merely fast. THE CHANGE AND WHY ITS JUSTIFICATION MATTERS MORE THAN USUAL. An earlier attempt at this node was stopped before committing because its brief carried a reason a peer measurement falsified while the node ran. Landing a falsified justification into the worker contract is worse than landing one into a plan: the contract is what a worker is told to follow, and a later reader who measures the wrong claim will find no effect and discard a control that works. THE MEASUREMENT, from a peer session that instrumented write position against each run's DECLARED deliverable paths across eight report-shaped nodes on one lane. Four total losses: three never touched their deliverable at all, and a fourth created it once at 0.7 percent of its life and never returned. Three landings wrote their deliverable across spans of 0.10 to 0.98, 0.03 to 1.00, and 0.94 to 1.00 of their lives. THAT THIRD ONE IS THE REFUTATION AND MUST APPEAR IN THE FILE: it wrote its deliverable entirely inside the final 6 percent of its run, a closing generation by any definition, and it landed cleanly. So a closing generation is not fatal, and writing incrementally does not predict survival. Note also the peer's methodological warning, which the file should carry in one clause: their first instrument counted every write including scratch files and separated nothing, because a node that writes ten scratch scripts and no report scores as incremental by write count. Filtering to the declared deliverable is what makes the measurement discriminate. WHAT THE MEASUREMENT DOES ESTABLISH, and this is the reason to state. Every total loss never wrote its deliverable at all. So the discriminator is whether a run reached its writing phase, not how it wrote once there — and a run that dies before that phase leaves nothing to recover. Two nodes in the same wave survived partially for exactly this reason: one wrote its findings into its manifest before the report it never produced, and all six findings were later re-measured as exact; another committed before dying, so the commit survived. A separate fleet reported four rescues with deliverables already on disk for the same reason. WHAT TO WRITE. State that a worker commits at each deliverable rather than once at the end, and writes its manifest before beginning any long output. State the reason as LOSS RECOVERY: a durable write that precedes a long generation survives that generation failing, and every total loss measured had never written its deliverable at all. State explicitly that this does not prevent deaths and is not expected to, naming the node that wrote its deliverable in the final 6 percent and landed, so a reader who measures death-reduction finds the claim already disclaimed rather than discovering it and discarding the practice. Connect to the existing rule that long output goes in the file and the reply is the path rather than restating it. WHAT NOT TO CHANGE. Do not alter the eight node properties or their order. Do not alter the manifest-path section, the delivery section, or the fence descriptions. Do not add a rate-based abort rule, a turn-count limit or a context-size limit: tokens per second was measured on 14 runs and did not reproduce on 26, and turn count and cumulative input were measured and separate nothing, so the file must not acquire a threshold the data refutes. Do not claim incremental writing improves survival. Do not name a backend, a model or a lane: the property is about where the durable write falls relative to the long output. FALSIFIERS. The refuting node is named with its final-6-percent span and its clean landing. The declared-deliverable filtering clause is present. The words tokens per second, turn limit and context limit appear nowhere as a rule. No backend or model name appears in the added text. node_definition.done_when: pytest tests/test_quota_weight.py -q passes, and a function in a new module converts a run's model identity and its token quantities into a relative quota weight that discriminates the members of one metered model family, refusing rather than defaulting for a model it has no declared rate for. WHY. This fleet routes almost everything to one member of a metered family and is struggling with its weekly ceiling, while two cheaper members of the same family are measured as finishing comparable nodes. Nothing in the harness records how much quota a run actually consumed relative to another, so every routing argument is currently made on wall clock, which is not what a quota is spent in. The figures below were read from the vendor's published rate card and must be carried in the module as a declared table with the reason beside it, because a rate this table gets wrong silently misroutes every future node. THE DECLARED RATES, per million tokens, as published. The family's strongest member: input 4.00, output 20.00. Its middle member: input 2.00, output 12.00. Its efficient member: input 0.20, output 1.20. So relative to the strongest member, the middle member costs half on input and three fifths on output, and the efficient member costs one twentieth on input and six hundredths on output. There is a fourth, smaller member this project also dispatches to, on a separate quota, for which NO published rate was found; it must return the explicit refusal below rather than be assigned a plausible number. THE SURCHARGE, which is the part no surface here models. A request whose input exceeds 272,000 tokens is charged at twice input and one and a half times output FOR THE WHOLE REQUEST, not for the tokens above the line. So the weight depends on how many of a run's requests crossed that line, which is not derivable from a cumulative total: eighty requests of 200,000 tokens sum to sixteen million and cross nothing, two requests of 300,000 sum to 600,000 and cross twice. Take the threshold and both multipliers as named module-level constants with the published rule in a comment. WHAT TO BUILD, IN A NEW MODULE ONLY. Create reckon/crew/quota_weight.py exposing one function taking a model identifier, cumulative input tokens, cumulative output tokens, and the number of requests whose input crossed the threshold, and returning the relative weight together with the rate entry it used and whether the surcharge was applied. Do not import from reckon.crew.metering, which a peer is writing this hour; take plain numbers so this module is testable and reviewable on its own. Do not wire it into promotion, dispatch, the ledger, the CLI or any surface. Do not read any ledger file. THE UNIT MUST BE STATED AND MUST NOT BE DOLLARS. This project's workers run on a subscription, and the vendor states explicitly that a subscription is not priced per token; the published rates are the token-denominated billing surface and are being used here only as a RATIO between family members. So the function returns a dimensionless weight relative to the family's strongest member at one, never a currency amount, and the module docstring must say that in one sentence and say why. A corroborating figure worth recording in the same docstring: the subscription's own per-window message allowances for these three members stand in a ratio of roughly one to two to twenty, which agrees in direction and in order of magnitude with the token ratio, so the two independent denominations do not contradict each other. AN UNDECLARED MODEL IS A REFUSAL, NOT A DEFAULT. A model identifier absent from the declared table returns an explicit unknown carrying the identifier it could not price, and the caller can see that it was not priced. Never fall back to the strongest member's rate, never fall back to an average, and never return zero: this project has a standing rule that a free or unmeasured lane recorded as zero cost makes it look like the dearest or the cheapest lane on any surface that ranks by cost, and the existing ledger deliberately nulls and flags such a value rather than imputing it. Follow that precedent. FALSIFIERS, asserted in tests/test_quota_weight.py, every expected figure computed in the test from the declared constants rather than written as a literal. Equal token quantities across the three declared members return weights in the published ratio, with the strongest member's weight exactly one. THE ORDERING IS STRICT: for any identical non-zero token quantities the middle member's weight is strictly less than the strongest member's and the efficient member's is strictly less than the middle member's, so a future rate edit that accidentally inverts the family is caught. A run with zero requests over the threshold and a run with one differ by exactly the surcharge the constants declare, and the surcharged weight is strictly greater. A run whose cumulative input is sixteen million across many small requests, with zero crossings, weighs LESS than a run whose cumulative input is six hundred thousand across two crossing requests on the same model, asserted against figures the test computes, because this is the case a cumulative-only reading gets backwards and the whole reason the crossing count is a parameter. An undeclared model identifier returns the unknown marker, carries the identifier, and does not raise. An undeclared model does not return zero and does not return the same value as any declared member, asserted directly. Zero tokens on a declared model returns zero weight, since nothing was consumed, and this is distinguishable from the undeclared unknown. A negative token count raises rather than returning a negative weight. Measure base and head over the new file and the tests that import reckon.crew, report failure ids either side, require none added, bound the run per file, and never run the full suite for this node.

node_definition.done_when: pytest tests/test_input_token_quantities.py -q passes, and the throughput block a run records carries the largest single request's input tokens and the run's cumulative input tokens in two separately named fields, with neither dialect ever filling one from the other. WHY. reckon/_backends.py has one field, peak_input_tokens, carrying two different quantities depending on which backend wrote the row, and the module states the rule it breaks in its own docstring. The method that serves the claude and clive dialects says, verbatim: Peak input is the largest single prompt the run sent, which is the figure a context window is actually spent against; the cumulative totals on the result are the sum over every request and would read far past any window. The method that serves the codex dialect then computes peak_input as a SUM over the run's usage counters, input tokens plus cached input tokens, and stores that sum in the field named peak. Measured across 3,269 ledger rows in the mounted projects: the codex figure has a median of 16,385,195 and a maximum of 106,803,531 while the clive figure's median is 171,518 and claude-opus's is 135,558. No context window is sixteen million tokens, so the codex column is not a peak and every surface that reads it as one is wrong. WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND TIDINESS. A published rule charges a request whose input exceeds 272,000 tokens at twice input and one and a half times output for the whole request, so the largest single request is what decides whether a run paid a surcharge, and the sum cannot answer it in either direction: eighty requests of 200,000 sum to sixteen million and never cross, two requests of 300,000 sum to 600,000 and cross twice. Both shapes occur here. Separately, input_utilisation_pct is computed from this field against the input budget, so on any dialect where the field holds a sum that percentage is a cumulative-over-window ratio and means nothing. WHAT TO CHANGE. Give the shared throughput block a cumulative input field and a cumulative cached input field alongside the existing peak field, defaulting to the unmeasured marker the block already uses for everything it did not measure, and thread them through the block constructor and the block that admits it measured nothing so both shapes carry the same keys. In the codex dialect, record the summed counters into the cumulative fields where they belong, and record the peak field as the unmeasured marker rather than as the sum, because that dialect's result does not report a per-request maximum and an honest absence is worth more than a wrong number. Do not attempt to derive the per-request maximum here: it needs a walk over per-turn records, another node owns that, and guessing it in this file is how the present defect was introduced. In the claude and clive dialect, keep the existing peak derivation exactly as it is and populate the cumulative fields from the result's own cumulative totals if and only if the result reports them; where it does not, leave them unmeasured. Compute input_utilisation_pct from the peak field only, so it becomes unmeasured on the codex dialect rather than misleading, and say why in a comment at the computation. WHAT NOT TO CHANGE. Do not touch reckon/crew/promotion.py or reckon/crew/prompts.py, both held by peers. Do not rewrite existing ledger rows or add a migration: the historical codex column keeps its recorded value under whatever name the field ends up with, and a reader of old rows is served by the finding being documented, not by a rewrite this node cannot verify. Do not add the surcharge multiplier or any cost arithmetic; this node records quantities and another owns their price. FALSIFIERS, asserted in tests/test_input_token_quantities.py. A constructed codex-dialect stream carrying known input, cached input and output counters produces a throughput block whose cumulative input equals the sum the test computes from those counters, whose cumulative cached input equals the cached counter, and WHOSE PEAK INPUT FIELD IS THE UNMEASURED MARKER, so the sum can never again be read as a peak. A constructed claude-dialect stream with three assistant turns of differing input sizes produces a peak input equal to the largest of the three and not their sum, asserted against figures the test computes. The block returned by the constructor and the block that admits it measured nothing carry exactly the same set of keys, asserted by comparing the key sets, so no reader meets a block missing a field. input_utilisation_pct is the unmeasured marker whenever the peak field is unmeasured, even when a cumulative figure and an input budget are both present, so the ratio cannot be computed from the wrong numerator. A block where peak input is present and below the input budget still reports the same percentage it reports today, asserted against a figure the test computes, so the existing meaning is unchanged on the dialect that was correct. Every existing test that asserts on a throughput block still passes: run the tests that import the backends module and the tests that assert on ledger throughput rows, measure base and head over that set, report failure ids either side, and require none added. Bound the run per file rather than issuing one census, and never run the full suite for this node.

Two of those three gaps closed today and the third turned out to be a naming defect rather than an absence. A finding nobody can read is not a finding. THE FIGURES TO RECORD, all of them given here so you do not need to search for or verify any of them; you have no network access and must not attempt to obtain them. Published per million tokens: the family's strongest member, input 4.00 and output 20.00; the middle member, input 2.00 and output 12.00; the efficient member, input 0.20 and output 1.20. Published surcharge: a request whose input exceeds 272,000 tokens is charged at twice input and one and a half times output for the WHOLE request, not for the tokens above the line; the family's raw context window is 372,000 with an effective figure near 353,400, so a default configuration carries roughly 81,400 tokens of exposure above the threshold, and the documented workaround is a client setting capping auto-compaction at 270,000. Published per-window message allowances on the subscription tier this project uses, which are a SECOND and independent denomination: roughly 200 to 2,000 for the strongest member, 500 to 4,000 for the middle, 5,000 to 40,000 for the efficient one, a ratio near one to two to twenty that agrees with the token ratio in direction and order of magnitude. Record explicitly that the vendor states a subscription is not priced per token, so the rates are being used as ratios between family members and never as a currency amount charged to this project. MEASURED HERE, from 3,269 rows across the mounted project ledgers: the strongest member's recorded input figure has a median of 16,385,195 and a maximum of 106,803,531 over 305 rows carrying it; the middle member 8,862,849 median over 15 rows; the efficient member 8,354,435 median over 14 rows; the local unmetered lane 171,518 median over 200 rows; one claude lane 135,558 median over 66 rows. Record that the cached prefix counts toward the threshold, so a run with a high cache-hit rate is MORE likely to be paying the surcharge rather than less, which turns a previously recorded linear cost in cached tokens into a step function at 272,000. Record that any comparison of that field ACROSS dialects is a maximum against a total and is invalid. WHAT NOT TO DO. Do not edit any file under reckon/ or tests/; three peers hold source this hour. Do not restate or relitigate the existing content of the document beyond what is needed to correct the UNMEASURED claim where it is now false; add your section and amend that specific claim, leaving the rest of the prose alone. Do not add a figure that is not either in this brief or read by you from the mounted ledgers, and label which of the two every number came from. WHY THIS IS THE BLOCKING GAP. Every routing and cost decision this fleet is making rests on tokens per durable node, and the ledger records a PEAK input figure and no cumulative one. A peer session derived it by hand from stream records for four runs and produced figures that reversed the conclusion an aggregate had suggested, which is the evidence that the quantity matters and that it is derivable. WHAT THE TWO DIALECTS LOOK LIKE. One dialect reports per-turn usage on assistant messages, carrying input tokens, output tokens and cache-read input tokens as separate counters. The other reports completed items rather than messages and carries its usage in a different shape; a peer's first instrument handled only the first dialect and would have reported every run on the second as having consumed nothing, which is a false zero that would have confirmed the hypothesis it was built to test. Read both. Determine each dialect's shape from real streams under the crew runs directory rather than from an assumption, and state in a comment which record and which field each dialect's figure comes from, so a later reader can reproduce the number without rediscovering the shape. Do not wire it into promotion, dispatch, the ledger or any command: promotion is held by another worker and this node's value is the deriver plus its proof. Where a dialect reports cached input separately from fresh input, state in a comment whether the returned cumulative input includes cached tokens and why. The reason to include them is that the meter on at least one metered lane charges total input including cached, which this project has recorded; the reason a reader might expect otherwise is that a cache hit feels free. Return both figures separately as well as the total, so a caller can choose and no caller has to guess which convention was used. AN UNMEASURABLE STREAM IS NOT A ZERO. node_definition.done_when: pytest tests/test_rollout_receipt.py -q passes, and a function in a new module reads, for one run identified by its session id, the quota and token receipt the metered client already writes to its own per-session rollout file: the run's true cumulative input across every turn, the largest single request it sent, how many of its requests exceeded 272,000 input tokens, the effective context window the client reported, and the run's position in its rolling quota window. WHY THIS IS THE MOST VALUABLE NODE AVAILABLE. This fleet is rationing a weekly quota and has been reasoning about it from wall clock and from a mislabelled token column, while the client has been writing the actual quota reading into a file on this machine on every single request. Nothing in this project reads that file. A peer established the route this hour and it is verified: the client keeps one rollout file per session under its own sessions directory, the file name contains the crew session id verbatim, and its records carry the figures below. This is not a modelled cost, it is the vendor's own accounting handed to us. THE RECORD SHAPE, verified on this host so you do not need to discover it, though you must confirm it rather than trust me. Records of interest have a payload whose type is token_count. That payload carries an info object holding total_token_usage and last_token_usage, each with input_tokens, cached_input_tokens, cache_write_input_tokens, output_tokens, reasoning_output_tokens and total_tokens; info also carries model_context_window. The payload additionally carries a rate_limits object with a primary object holding used_percent, window_minutes and resets_at, and a credits object. Measured: window_minutes is 10080, which is seven days, so primary is the weekly quota and used_percent is our position in it. total_token_usage is the run's running total across every turn, which is the figure a peer proved the existing ledger column understates on any resumed run, and last_token_usage is the most recent single request, which is the figure this dialect's crew stream cannot supply at all. WHAT TO BUILD, IN A NEW MODULE ONLY. Create reckon/crew/rollout.py exposing one function that takes a session id, locates that session's rollout file, and returns the cumulative input, cumulative cached input and cumulative output from the LAST total_token_usage record; the maximum input over every last_token_usage record; the count of last_token_usage records whose input exceeded the threshold; the effective context window; and the quota window's used_percent, window_minutes and reset time from the last record that carries them. Take the threshold as a named module constant with its published rule in a comment. Do not wire it into promotion, dispatch, the ledger, the CLI or any surface. Do not read or modify any configuration file. Do not edit reckon/_backends.py, reckon/crew/metering.py, reckon/crew/quota_weight.py, reckon/crew/context_budget.py, reckon/crew/promotion.py, reckon/crew/prompts.py or docs/research/deploy-matrix.html; peers hold all seven this hour. THE BOUNDARY WITH A PEER, so you do not duplicate it: another node derives cumulative tokens from the CREW STREAM and correctly reports the per-request maximum as unmeasurable there. Your module reads the CLIENT'S ROLLOUT instead, which does carry it. Both are correct and they are different surfaces; say so in your docstring and name the other surface, so a reader meeting one knows the other exists. THE QUANTISATION CAVEAT IS PART OF THE DELIVERABLE, NOT A FOOTNOTE. Measured across twenty-four runs today, used_percent is reported only as whole numbers, so a single run's consumption comes back as zero, one, two or three points and a run that truly cost four tenths of a point is indistinguishable from one that cost nothing. Per-run attribution from this field is therefore not sound and per-model aggregates over many runs are. State that in the docstring in those terms, and return the raw reading rather than a computed per-run delta, so no caller can accidentally attribute a single run's burn from a quantised figure. This project already carries the same reasoning elsewhere for a burn projection floor: below a few percent of a window, quantisation dominates the measurement. Do not invent a floor here; just refuse to compute the delta. AN ABSENT RECEIPT IS NOT A ZERO. A session id with no rollout file, a rollout file that cannot be read, a file carrying no token_count record, and a file whose records carry no rate limits are four different states and must not collapse into one another or into zero. Return an explicit unmeasured marker for each figure the file does not support, and never return zero for a figure that was not measured: a quota reading of zero means an untouched window and is a real and different fact from an unread file. FALSIFIERS, asserted in tests/test_rollout_receipt.py, every expected figure computed in the test rather than written as a literal, and every fixture constructed rather than borrowed from a real session except where stated. A constructed rollout whose last_token_usage records carry differing input sizes returns the LARGEST, not the first, not the last, and not their sum, asserted against a fixture whose total is much larger than its maximum so a sum cannot pass. A constructed rollout carrying three requests above the threshold and four below returns three. A constructed rollout with several total_token_usage records returns the LAST one's figures, not the first and not a sum of them, since the field is already cumulative and summing it would double count; assert against a fixture whose earlier totals are smaller. The returned maximum single request is strictly less than the returned cumulative input on any fixture with more than one request, which is an arithmetic invariant and catches a confusion between the two objects. A missing session id, an unreadable file and a file with no token_count record each return the unmeasured markers and do not raise. A constructed rollout reporting a used_percent of zero returns zero and NOT the unmeasured marker, asserted directly against the unmeasured case, because those two are the states this project most often conflates. RANGE ONE FALSIFIER OVER THE REAL POPULATION, deliberately: run the function over at least twelve real session ids taken from this project's own ledger rows, assert it raises on none, and assert that for every run where both figures are measured the maximum single request does not exceed the reported effective context window, which is a physical invariant and the strongest available check that you are reading the right field. Report how many of the twelve had a rollout file at all, because a low hit rate is itself a finding about retention. Measure base and head over the new file and the tests that import reckon.crew, report failure ids either side, require none added, bound the run per file, and never run the full suite for this node.

node_definition.done_when: pytest tests/test_quota_weight.py -q passes, and the weight the module returns is proportional to what a run actually consumed rather than to its consumption per token, with the long-context surcharge applied to the tokens inside each crossing request rather than to the whole run. WHY THIS IS A REPAIR AND WHOSE FAULT IT IS. You built exactly what the previous contract specified and eleven tests pass; the contract was wrong in two ways and one of its falsifiers was inverted and passed only because of the first error. Both are the coordinator's, not yours. The module, the declared rate table, the strict family ordering and the explicit refusal for an undeclared model are all correct and land unchanged; only the arithmetic and the signature change. THE FIRST ERROR: THE FIGURE IS AN INTENSITY, NOT A COST. The helper divides the weighted token total by the token total, so a run of sixteen million tokens and a run of six hundred thousand tokens on the same model with the same mix return the SAME weight. A figure that cannot distinguish those two cannot rank anything, and ranking runs by consumption is the only reason this module exists. Return a figure proportional to the run's size: the weighted token total itself, unnormalised, still expressed relative to the reference member's rate so it stays dimensionless and is not a currency amount. Keep the reference member's RATE ratio at one; do not keep any run's weight at one. THE SECOND ERROR: THE SURCHARGE CANNOT BE COMPUTED FROM A COUNT. The published rule charges a request whose input exceeds the threshold at twice input and one and a half times output FOR THAT REQUEST. The current model instead multiplies the whole run's tokens by one plus the crossing count, so two crossings charge three times on every token in the run, including the tokens of requests that never crossed. On a sixteen-million-token run with two crossings that overstates by roughly a factor of three. A crossing count carries no information about how many tokens were inside the crossing requests, so no correct arithmetic can be built from it. CHANGE THE SIGNATURE ACCORDINGLY. Take the model identifier and a sequence of per-request figures, each carrying that request's input tokens and output tokens. Sum the run yourself: for each request, if its input exceeds the threshold apply the surcharge multipliers to that request's own input and output, otherwise apply neither, then weight by the model's rate ratio and add it in. Return the total weight, the rate entry used, the number of requests that crossed, and the token totals with and without the surcharge applied so a caller can see the surcharge's size rather than infer it. Do not accept a bare cumulative total plus a crossing count in any form: the point of the change is that the pair is insufficient, and an optional path taking it would be used. THE PER-REQUEST FIGURES EXIST, so this signature is not a burden on the caller. A peer node landing this hour reads the metered client's own per-session receipt file, whose records carry each request's input and output tokens individually; that is where a caller obtains the sequence. Do not import that module and do not read any file yourself — take plain numbers, so this module stays reviewable on its own — but name that surface in the docstring as the source of the sequence, so a reader knows the signature is satisfiable. FALSIFIERS, in tests/test_quota_weight.py, every expected figure computed in the test from the declared constants rather than written as a literal. Keep every existing test that still holds: the rate ratios for equal quantities, the strict family ordering, the undeclared-model refusal, the known zero, and the negative-input refusal. Delete the inverted comparison test outright and replace it with the correct direction: a run of sixteen million input tokens across many requests none of which crosses weighs STRICTLY MORE than a run of six hundred thousand input tokens across two requests that both cross, because sixteen million tokens at the plain rate exceeds six hundred thousand at twice the rate, and the previous contract asserted the reverse. THE SCALE FALSIFIER, which is the one that catches the normalisation returning: two runs on the same model with the same per-request mix, one exactly ten times the other in request count, return weights whose ratio is ten, asserted against a ratio the test computes. A normalised implementation returns one and fails this. THE PER-REQUEST ATTRIBUTION FALSIFIER: a run of two requests where only one crosses weighs strictly less than a run of the same two requests where both cross, and strictly more than the same two where neither does, with all three figures computed in the test; and the surcharge applied to a run whose crossing request is a small fraction of its tokens changes the total weight by strictly less than the surcharge applied to a run whose crossing request is most of its tokens, which is the property the count-based model could not express at all. An empty request sequence returns a known zero rather than the undeclared-model unknown. A request with a negative token count raises. A request whose input exactly equals the threshold does NOT cross, since the rule is strictly greater, and assert that boundary directly in both directions at the threshold and at the threshold plus one. Measure base and head over the changed file and the tests that import reckon.crew, report failure ids either side, require none added, bound the run per file, and never run the full suite for this node.

node_definition.done_when: pytest tests/test_lane_evidence.py -q passes, and a function in a new module returns, for a stated node shape, one row per lane carrying the three metrics that discriminate lanes plus the sample size behind each, refusing to report any figure whose sample is below a declared floor. WHY THESE THREE AND NOT THE OBVIOUS ONE. An orchestrator choosing a lane today has wall clock and folklore. The obvious metric, gate pass rate, CANNOT route and must be excluded with its reason stated in the module docstring: the worker writes its own gate, so the rate is saturated between 0.93 and 1.00 across every lane measured in this project and carries almost no information. Three metrics do discriminate and all three are derivable from the ledger rows this project already commits. FIRST, REWORK. A durable node is one whose run promoted with a commit. A node is reworked when a LATER run re-touches any path the earlier run declared as a write path. Measured previously in this project, rework discriminates about eight times more strongly than gate pass and reverses the cost ordering: one lane looks 34 percent cheaper on gate pass and is 22 percent dearer per durable node once rework is counted. Compute rework by comparing declared write paths across rows ordered by dispatch time, and exclude a row's own attempts and its own shadows from counting as rework of itself, since a retry of one node is not the next node redoing it. SECOND, OVERCLAIM, which is the metric today's evidence most needs and which nothing computes. A row overclaims when the worker's manifest reported a terminal success while the coordinator's recorded outcome says the done-when was not met. The rows carry both: the manifest status, and the promoted outcome and failure classification. Count a row as overclaiming when its manifest status was complete or passed and its promoted classification is work-rejected, or when its outcome text records that a named part of the done-when was absent, unexecuted or not delivered. Do not attempt to judge the work yourself and do not parse the done-when; read only what the coordinator recorded. This is the metric that separates a lane that stops and says so from a lane that stops and reports complete, and those two failure shapes need opposite handling from an orchestrator. THIRD, COST PER DURABLE NODE, expressed in the dimensionless lane weight this project already declares rather than in currency, since the workers run on a subscription that is not priced per token. Take the weight from the existing reckon.crew.quota_weight module; do not recompute any rate and do not import reckon.crew.rollout or reckon.crew.metering, whose figures are not yet on the rows. Where a row carries no token quantities, the cost for that row is unmeasured and it must not be counted as zero, because a lane with unmeasured rows would otherwise rank as the cheapest. Report wall seconds per durable node beside it as the fourth column, since wall and quota are different scarce things and an orchestrator trades them against each other. CONDITION EVERY ROW ON NODE SHAPE, because the premise of the whole surface is that the best lane depends on the work. Take the shape as the role and the specification level, and return only rows matching them, so a caller asking about exact implementation nodes is not shown an aggregate dominated by open-ended documentation work. Report the shape back in the result so a reader cannot mistake which population they are looking at. THE SAMPLE FLOOR IS THE DESIGN, NOT A GUARD. Declare a module-level minimum sample and return, for any lane below it, an explicit insufficient-evidence marker naming the count it has, rather than a figure. State in the docstring that a rate over three rows is not evidence and that publishing one invites a decision the data cannot support; this project has already had a lane comparison rest on five rows across three lanes and a determinism result rest on two measurements that were secretly identical. A surface that refuses is what makes the numbers it does report trustworthy. WHAT TO BUILD AND WHAT NOT TO. Create reckon/crew/lane_evidence.py exposing one function taking the ledger rows, a role and a specification level, and returning the rows described above plus the shape it filtered on. Read rows through the existing ledger reader rather than opening any file yourself. Do NOT register a command-line entry point in this node: reckon/cli.py is held by a peer this hour and a sequenced follow-up owns the command, which is stated here so the absence reads as sequencing rather than oversight. Do not select a lane, rank the rows, or emit a recommendation of any kind: the orchestrator decides and this surface informs, and a module that picks would hide exactly the decision this design exists to expose. Say that in the docstring. Do not touch reckon/crew/dispatch.py, reckon/cli.py, reckon/ledger.py, reckon/crew/quota_weight.py, reckon/crew/rollout.py or reckon/crew/context_budget.py; peers hold all six. FALSIFIERS, in tests/test_lane_evidence.py, every expected figure computed in the test from its own fixture rows rather than written as a literal, and every fixture synthesised rather than read from a real ledger. Two lanes with identical gate outcomes but different rework counts return different rework rates, which is the property gate pass cannot express. A later row re-touching an earlier row's declared write path counts as rework of that earlier row; a retry attempt of the same node does not; a shadow of the same node does not. A row whose manifest said complete and whose promoted classification is work-rejected counts as an overclaim, and a row that blocked and said so does not, asserted side by side so the two failure shapes are provably distinguished. A lane whose rows carry no token quantities reports its cost as unmeasured and NOT as zero, asserted directly against a lane with real quantities so the two cannot compare equal. A lane with fewer rows than the declared floor returns the insufficient-evidence marker carrying its actual count, and a lane at exactly the floor returns figures, so the boundary is pinned in both directions. A caller asking for one role and specification level receives no row derived from any other shape, asserted by including rows of a second shape in the fixture and requiring they contribute nothing to any figure. The returned result names the shape it filtered on. An empty row set returns insufficient evidence for every lane rather than raising or returning an empty success. Measure base and head over the new file and the tests that import reckon.crew, report failure ids either side, require none added, bound the run per file, and never run the full suite for this node.

node_definition.done_when: pytest tests/test_context_budget.py -q passes, and a function in a new module reports, for one run's stream, how many times that run's history was compacted and the largest context size the stream reveals it reached, distinguishing a run that never compacted because it was short from one that never reached the ceiling from one whose stream cannot answer. WHY THIS IS WORTH A NODE. The metered family this fleet dispatches to documents a window near one million tokens while the client ships a much lower tuned default, so until an hour ago every worker here compacted at roughly a third of the model's capability. That default has now been raised in the host configuration. Two things are now unknown and both are decision-relevant. First, whether the raise is honoured at all: published guidance warns that some subscription accounts hit an effective ceiling near 360,000 tokens REGARDLESS of the configured value, and that figure is suspiciously close to the client's own default effective window, so it may describe accounts whose config never took effect rather than a server cap. If our account is capped, a client that believes it has a million tokens will not compact and the request will fail at the server instead, which is worse than compacting. Second, how often we were compacting before, because compaction costs turns and a re-oriented worker re-reads files, and this project has measured that burn is steps multiplied by context. Neither figure exists anywhere today. WHAT THE STREAM MIGHT CARRY, AND YOU MUST DETERMINE IT RATHER THAN ASSUME IT. A peer established this morning that this dialect's streams carry many completed-item records with no usage on them and exactly one aggregate usage record for the whole turn, so per-request token figures are not available. What is NOT yet established is whether the client emits anything when it compacts history, or when it approaches or hits a context ceiling. Find out from real streams under the crew runs directory: there are hundreds, spanning short runs and runs of many hours, and the long ones must have compacted repeatedly under the old default. Search for records whose type or content concerns compaction, context, history, truncation, summarisation or a token limit, and read the actual records rather than matching on a word. If such a record exists it is the most valuable thing in this node, because the context size at the moment of compaction is the ONLY route this dialect offers to a per-request-scale figure, and that figure is what settles the ceiling question. WHAT TO BUILD, IN A NEW MODULE ONLY. Create reckon/crew/context_budget.py exposing one function taking a path to a run's stream and returning the number of compactions observed, the largest context size the stream reveals, the record type each figure was read from, and an explicit unmeasured marker for any figure the stream does not support. Do not wire it into promotion, dispatch, the ledger, the CLI or any surface. Do not read or modify any configuration file. Do not edit reckon/_backends.py, reckon/crew/metering.py, reckon/crew/quota_weight.py, reckon/crew/promotion.py, reckon/crew/prompts.py or docs/research/deploy-matrix.html; peers hold all six this hour. IF THE STREAM CARRIES NO SUCH RECORD, THAT IS THE FINDING AND YOU DELIVER IT. Return the unmeasured marker for both figures on this dialect, state in a comment which record types you searched and how many records of each you examined, and give the count of streams and records you looked at so a later reader can judge the search rather than repeat it. A negative result stated with its search breadth is a real deliverable here; a negative result stated without it is worthless. Do not substitute the aggregate turn usage for a context size — a peer blocked correctly this morning rather than make exactly that substitution, because relabelling a run total as a per-request figure is the defect this work exists to remove. RANGE THE FALSIFIERS OVER THE DOMAIN, NOT OVER THE STREAMS YOU FIND. Every real stream available to you was produced under the OLD configuration, so a test asserting only against real streams ranges over a population in which the new behaviour cannot appear, and this project has shipped a fail-open past a clean suite for exactly that reason. So construct streams for the cases reality cannot yet supply. FALSIFIERS, asserted in tests/test_context_budget.py, every expected figure computed in the test rather than written as a literal. A constructed stream containing three compaction records returns three, and one containing none returns zero rather than the unmeasured marker, so a run that genuinely did not compact is distinguishable from a stream that cannot say. A constructed stream carrying no record of any relevant type returns the unmeasured marker for both figures and does not raise. A missing stream path and an unreadable stream both return the unmeasured marker and do not raise. A constructed stream whose compaction records carry differing context sizes returns the largest, not the first, not the last and not their sum. The largest context size returned is never equal to a cumulative or aggregate total present in the same constructed stream, asserted directly by placing a much larger aggregate figure in the fixture and requiring the returned figure to be the smaller per-compaction one, so the substitution that blocked the peer node cannot pass here either. Run the function over at least twenty real streams of varying length and assert it raises on none of them and returns a coherent result for each, which is a robustness check and not a claim about the figures. Measure base and head over the new file and the tests that import reckon.crew, report failure ids either side, require none added, bound the run per file, and never run the full suite for this node.

THE EXACT CURRENT STATE, measured, so you do not need to search for it. reckon/ledger.py line 91 opens a module-level tuple named RECORD_FIELDS holding 36 string entries. Grepping the whole package for that name returns exactly one hit, its own definition line: nothing reads it. Meanwhile promoted rows across the mounted project ledgers carry 50 distinct keys, so the tuple that reads as the record schema is fourteen keys behind what is written and nothing would ever have said so. THE FOURTEEN MISSING KEYS, with the number of rows carrying each, which is the complete list and the only list: execution_fit on 2141 rows, attempt_kind on 2105, attempt on 2105, throughput on 705, worktree_retention on 559, no_commit on 303, dispute_count on 258, follow_on_paths on 254, scope_acceptances on 23, resume_waiver on 17, watch_override on 13, predecessor_run on 10, boundary_waiver on 3, commit_resolution on 2. Place each one beside the declared key it belongs with rather than appending all fourteen at the end: attempt and attempt_kind near the dispatch identity keys, execution_fit near role and spec_level, throughput near wall_seconds and worker_seconds, no_commit and commit_resolution near commits, scope_acceptances near scope_changed, boundary_waiver and resume_waiver and watch_override and unreconciled_override together as the waivers, follow_on_paths and dispute_count and predecessor_run and worktree_retention near the outcome keys. Grouping is the whole value of the tuple to a reader, so do not sort it and do not append. Add one short comment above the tuple saying what the tuple is for and that a test holds it complete. Do not reorder or rename any key that is already declared. Do not change any other file. WHAT NOT TO DO. Do not delete the tuple even though nothing reads it; the test below is what gives it a job. Do not wire it into serialisation, validation, promotion or any writer: a tuple that starts filtering rows would silently drop any key it does not list, which is a far worse defect than the one you are fixing, and this node must not create it. Do not touch reckon/_backends.py, reckon/crew/quota_weight.py, reckon/crew/rollout.py or reckon/crew/context_budget.py; peers hold all four. Do not rewrite or migrate any ledger file. It must PASS after your change and it must be written so that it WOULD HAVE FAILED before it, naming those fourteen: prove that by also asserting each of the fourteen names above is present in RECORD_FIELDS, listed explicitly in the test. Assert RECORD_FIELDS contains no duplicate entries, by comparing its length to the length of a set built from it. Assert every entry is a non-empty string. Assert the count of declared keys is at least fifty, computed from the collected union rather than written as a literal, so the number moves with reality instead of becoming a fuse. When the collected union of keys is empty, meaning no ledger file was opened and parsed, the test calls pytest.skip with a message naming the mount paths it tried, rather than asserting a subset relation over an empty set, which would pass while measuring nothing. Assert the collected union is non-empty before the subset assertion so the skip is the only path that avoids it. Run pytest on the new test file alone and on tests/test_ledger.py, report the exit status and the pass and fail counts for each at base and at head, and require no added failures. node_definition.done_when: pytest tests/test_rollout_receipt.py -q passes, and the quota figures the receipt reader returns are keyed by the length of the window they describe rather than by the position they appear in, so a five-hour reading can never be reported as a weekly one. THE DEFECT, measured on this host within the last hour on freshly landed code. reckon/crew/rollout.py reads the rate limit block's primary entry and returns it as the run's quota position. That was written from a sample of one endpoint family, where primary carries the weekly window and secondary is null. A second family on the same account reports the OPPOSITE: primary carries used_percent 94.0 with window_minutes 300, which is five hours, and secondary carries used_percent 42.0 with window_minutes 10080, which is a week. Both entries were present and populated in one record. So the position in the block does not identify the window, and the current reader would publish a nearly exhausted five-hour figure as though it were a weekly one, understating the weekly by more than a factor of two while overstating urgency on the wrong horizon. This is the same shape of defect as a field that means a maximum on one dialect and a sum on another, and it is being reported here rather than discovered later because the code is new. WHAT THE RECORD ACTUALLY CARRIES, verified, so you need not guess: the rate limit block holds limit_id, limit_name, primary, secondary, credits, individual_limit, spend_control_reached, plan_type and rate_limit_reached_type. Each of primary and secondary, when present, holds used_percent, window_minutes and resets_at. Either may be null. WHAT TO CHANGE. Return the quota readings keyed by window length, not by position: read both primary and secondary wherever present, and expose each reading with its own window_minutes, used_percent and reset time, so a caller asks for the window it cares about rather than trusting an ordering. Provide a named accessor for the five-hour horizon and one for the weekly horizon that select by window length, and make each return the explicit unmeasured marker when no entry of that length is present, never the other entry and never a zero. Do not hardcode the two lengths as the only possibilities: select the weekly reading as the entry whose window is a week and the short-horizon reading as the entry whose window is materially shorter, and if the record ever carries a length matching neither, expose it under its own length rather than dropping it, because a silently dropped horizon is how this defect arose. Also return the effective context window already read, and the plan type, both of which vary by family and are decision-relevant: the two families measured here report 258,400 and 121,600 respectively. Keep every existing absence marker and keep a measured zero used_percent as zero. WHAT NOT TO DO. Do not aggregate the two horizons into a single number or a single worst-case figure: they are separate budgets with different reset times and an orchestrator needs both. Do not compute headroom, a verdict, or an availability judgement of any kind; this module reads a receipt. Do not read or modify any configuration file, and do not touch reckon/crew/dispatch.py, reckon/cli.py, reckon/crew/lane_evidence.py, reckon/crew/quota_weight.py, reckon/crew/metering.py or reckon/crew/context_budget.py; peers hold all six. FALSIFIERS, in tests/test_rollout_receipt.py, every fixture constructed and every expected figure computed in the test rather than written as a literal. Keep every existing test that still holds. A constructed record whose primary is a weekly window and whose secondary is null returns the weekly figure under the weekly accessor and the unmeasured marker under the short-horizon accessor. A constructed record whose primary is a five-hour window and whose secondary is weekly returns the SAME weekly figure under the weekly accessor as the previous fixture did, asserted by giving both fixtures identical weekly numbers in different positions and requiring identical results, which is the property that makes position irrelevant and is the exact defect being fixed. That same fixture returns the five-hour figure under the short-horizon accessor and NOT under the weekly one, asserted against the weekly value so the two can never be confused. A record whose two entries are both present and whose short-horizon utilisation is far higher than its weekly one returns both faithfully, so an exhausted short window does not mask an ample weekly budget or the reverse. A record carrying a window length matching neither horizon still exposes that reading under its own length and is not dropped, asserted by looking for the length in the result. WHY THIS IS THE GAP RATHER THAN MORE CODE. The mechanism landed today: a live dispatch can name its lane, a member's declared harness routes rather than being decorative, an unusable named lane refuses instead of falling back, and the requested lane is recorded beside the resolved one. None of that is written down anywhere an orchestrator reads, and today two peer fleets between them sent five consecutive nodes to one metered lane by omission, maintained rosters whose declarations had no routing authority when they were made, and discovered the working route by reading source. A mechanism nobody knows the rules for is the same defect as a guard that never runs. READ THE PLAN FOR ANYTHING SEMANTIC; DO NOT RESTATE IT. The plan sections named in this node's authority own which measures route, which are excluded and why, and any figure about lane cost or lane quality. Link to them or name them; do not copy a number or a verdict out of them into this reference, because a copy goes stale silently and a node on this very plan was blocked earlier today for exactly that reason. This reference documents the MECHANISM and the OPERATOR PROCEDURE only. WHAT THE REFERENCE MUST COVER, and all of the following is measured on this host today rather than proposed. How to name a lane on a live dispatch, with the option name, and that the same option exists on the shadow and resume commands so one vocabulary covers all three. That a named lane which flight config does not declare, or declares but cannot serve, is refused rather than quietly replaced by the default. That a roster member's declared harness now routes: a member declared for one lane will steer a dispatch to that lane, and the option and the declaration disagreeing is refused with both named. THE ROSTER RE-READ IS THE MOST URGENT PARAGRAPH IN THE FILE: declarations made while the field was decorative now carry routing authority, so a roster built before today steers dispatches it did not steer when it was built, and an orchestrator must list its roster and compare each member's declared harness against the lane it intends before its next wave. Give the command that lists it. Include the measured hazard in the direction that actually bites: one fleet holds roughly forty members declaring an unmetered local lane, and reusing one of those for a metered dispatch would now land on the local lane; the reverse mistake, sending metered work to a metered lane by omission, is the one everyone anticipates and the less likely of the two. That each run records the requested lane beside the resolved one, and that comparing those two fields is how a silent divergence is found in one read rather than by accident. THE PROCEDURE FOR WHEN THE CHOICE IS NOT OBVIOUS, stated as steps rather than as advice. Consult the selection evidence rather than folklore, naming the surfaces that carry it and saying plainly that one of them reports endpoint availability and quota horizons and is worth reading before choosing rather than after a refusal. Say that a lane with too few observations returns an explicit insufficient-evidence marker rather than a figure, that this is deliberate, and that the correct response to it is to generate an observation rather than to guess: dispatch the same node to two lanes and compare, which is what the shadow command exists for. Say that no surface selects a lane and none will, and give the reason in one sentence: the orchestrator owns the decision and a component that picked would hide it. Include the escalation shape as a numbered procedure: route to the cheaper lane first, and when it stops honestly, move the run to a stronger lane with the command that preserves its worktree, advising the successor to commit the inherited diff as a checkpoint before continuing. State that this works only because a lane that reports false completion can never be a first rung, and point at the plan for which measure establishes that. WHAT NOT TO DO. Do not put a model name, a lane ranking, a price, a token figure or a quota percentage in this file: every one of those moves, and a snapshot of a moving number in a reference is a fuse. Refer to lanes by the role they play in a procedure and let the evidence surfaces carry the values. Do not name any plan label, sprint, node, session, run or ticket identifier. node_definition.done_when: pytest tests/test_a_short_commit_list_is_reported.py -q passes, and a passing promotion presenting fewer commits than its own manifest declares is reported, naming both counts and the missing revisions. THE MEASUREMENT, arriving independently from three sessions across two fleets. One audited 720 ledger rows carrying both a commits list and a manifest commits line: 534 agree, 62 have a ledger list that is a strict SUBSET of the manifest's, and 124 disagree without being a subset. The worst subset case recorded 31 commits as one; another recorded 8 as 1. The 124 are the opposite defect, a worker manifest quoting a revision the coordinator declined in favour of the verified head, so there the presented list resolves and the manifest's does not. A naive mismatch count returns 186 and conflates the two, which would send a reader to the side whose record resolves on two thirds of the hits. THE CONSEQUENCE IS A DISABLED GUARD, NOT MERELY AN UNDER-RECORD. The out-of-scope boundary check runs against the commits a promotion presents, so an incomplete presentation silently switches it off: one reporting session had a scope extension reach the ledger with an empty acceptance list while the same check fired minutes later on a different node over a one-line test helper. WHAT ALREADY EXISTS AND WHY IT DOES NOT COVER THIS. reckon/crew/promotion.py already guards the commitless case: a passing verdict presenting no commits while the worktree head has moved off its base, and it consults the manifest's own commits line first for exactly this reason, with the measured incident recorded in its docstring. But its condition returns early whenever the presented list is non-empty, so a promotion presenting one commit where the manifest declares eight passes through untouched. The absence is caught and the shortfall is not. WHAT TO CHANGE. Extend that guard so a passing promotion whose presented commits are a strict subset of the manifest's declared commits is reported, naming how many were presented, how many the manifest declared, and which revisions are missing. Reuse the existing manifest commits reader rather than adding a second one. It reports and never refuses. The reporting sessions asked for refuse-or-warn and this node implements the warn half only, for a reason their own data supplies: 124 of their 720 rows have the manifest quoting a revision the coordinator declined in favour of one that resolves, so the manifest is not trustworthy enough to gate on, and a refusal keyed on it would block promotions whose presented list resolves at roughly twice the rate it caught incomplete ones. WHAT NOT TO CHANGE. Do not alter the existing commitless guard's behaviour or its message. Do not refuse any promotion. Do not treat a manifest revision absent from the repository as authoritative: a manifest may quote a revision that does not resolve, so verify each declared revision resolves in the run's repository before naming it as missing, and say nothing about one that does not resolve rather than reporting it as lost work. Do not report the non-subset case: the coordinator's list is right there and reporting it would name the list that resolves, which is the specific confusion the mismatch count causes. FALSIFIERS, asserted in tests/test_a_short_commit_list_is_reported.py against constructed manifests and a temporary repository. A promotion presenting one of three declared commits is reported, and the report names one, three, and the two missing revisions. A promotion presenting all declared commits is silent. A promotion presenting commits the manifest does not declare is silent, because that case is the coordinator having declined a worker's revision, where the presented list is the one that resolves in the repository. A promotion presenting a superset is silent. A manifest with no commits line at all is silent and does not raise. A declared revision that does not resolve in the repository is not named as missing, asserted with a well-formed forty-character revision that resolves to nothing. The existing commitless guard still fires on a passing promotion with an empty list whose worktree head moved off base, asserted unchanged. Nothing is refused: assert the promotion completes in every case above. Measure base and head over the new file plus every test importing reckon.crew.promotion; report failure ids either side and require none added, and bound the run per file rather than issuing one census.

WHY THIS IS THE PRIORITY. Orchestrators across thirteen mounted projects choose a lane before every dispatch and currently have no way to see whether a lane will even serve them. The information exists on this machine and is unreachable in practice: it sits in the metered client's per-session receipt file, whose location a caller must know, whose records must be filtered, and whose structure is NOT UNIFORM between endpoint families. Measured within the last hour, on this host, one family reports its weekly window in the block's primary entry with the secondary entry null, while a second family reports its FIVE-HOUR window in primary and its weekly in secondary. So a reader that trusts position publishes a five-hour figure as a weekly one; that mistake was made in this repository today and is being repaired in the receipt module by a peer this hour. A shared read is the structural fix; a shared convention is not, because every session would re-derive it and diverge. Measured figures that make the point concrete: one family sits at 94 percent of a 300-minute window and 42 percent of a 10080-minute window at the same instant, so a dispatch there will be refused within the hour while its weekly budget is ample; and the two families report effective context windows of 258,400 and 121,600, a factor of two, which is the single best predictor of whether a node fits its lane and appears nowhere else. WHERE TO GET THE DATA. Read the receipt through reckon.crew.rollout, never by opening a session file yourself. That module is being changed by a peer this hour to key its quota readings by window length. If it exposes accessors that select a reading by window length, use them.
