So the protocol reaches a worker only if something puts it in the prompt, and nothing does. The consequence was measured across three sessions this week, which independently reported the same class of manifest defect: manifests under-reporting real work, one reading commits pending over a real commit, one reading status complete with its declared artifact absent, three passed runs leaving commits and artifacts blank. One reporting coordinator stated the conclusion as only flight config is enforced, so only flight config is real, and then compensated by hand-writing the discipline into every brief's own done-when text for its next wave. That compensation is the evidence for this node: a coordinator should not have to retype a contract clause into every brief for it to reach a worker. THE DISTINCTION THAT MAKES THIS BELONG IN THE PROMPT RATHER THAN IN A BRIEF. The prompt's own docstring states its principle: anything the live plan already says is omitted, because the worker's first act is to read the plan. That principle is correct and this text does not violate it. Plan content is what THIS node must achieve and varies per node. Contract content is what EVERY node must do regardless of plan, and a worker that never reads the references cannot learn it from anywhere else. Commit-at-each-deliverable is contract content by that test: it is identical for every node reckon will ever dispatch. WHAT TO ADD, AND ITS STATED REASON. Add to the composed prompt that the worker commits each deliverable as it completes rather than once at the end, and writes its manifest carrying whatever it already holds before beginning any long output. State the reason as loss recovery and not as death prevention: a durable write preceding a long generation survives that generation failing. Do not claim it improves the chance of finishing, because that reading was measured and refuted on two fleets independently, one of which found a node that wrote its entire deliverable inside the final six percent of its run and landed cleanly. KEEP IT SHORT, BECAUSE SHORTNESS IS THE PROMPT'S DESIGN AND NOT AN ACCIDENT. The addition is at most four sentences. It names no backend, no model and no lane. It does not restate the manifest path rules, the fence descriptions or the delivery rule, all of which the prompt or the references already carry. WHAT NOT TO CHANGE. Do not add any other protocol text, however useful; a prompt that grows to hold the whole reference stops being read. Do not embed the references by file path or by inclusion, because a path in a prompt is an instruction to go and read, which is the failure this node exists to remove. Do not alter what the prompt says about the plan, the section, the write paths, the peers, the manifest path or the time budget. Do not add a rate limit, a turn limit or a context limit. FALSIFIERS, asserted in tests/test_the_prompt_carries_the_contract.py against a composed prompt built from a constructed node. The composed prompt contains the commit-at-each-deliverable instruction and the manifest-before-long-output instruction. Its stated reason is recovery, and the prompt does not assert that the practice prevents failure or improves completion. The added text is at most four sentences, asserted by counting. No backend, model or lane name appears in the addition. Every other element the prompt carried before is still present, asserted by composing the same node before and after and diffing, so the addition is purely additive. The prompt does not contain a filesystem path to any reference document. A node with no write paths and a node with several both receive the addition, so it is not conditional on shape. Measure base and head over the new file plus every test importing reckon.crew.prompts; report failure ids either side and require none added.
node_definition.goal: Put the commit-and-manifest-early contract into the composed dispatch prompt, so it reaches the worker rather than depending on a reference nothing embeds

node_definition.done_when: pytest tests/test_lanes_view_serving_state.py -q passes, and the lanes view's serving state distinguishes a lane with ample quota, a lane close enough to its ceiling that a dispatch is at risk, and a lane whose reading is too old to support any claim, rather than reporting that a lane will serve at every utilisation below the absolute ceiling. THE DEFECT, measured against the live route minutes after the view landed. reckon/mcp_views.py derives the serving state as exhausted when used percent is at or above one hundred and as will-serve for every other measured value. The utilisation figure is reported in WHOLE NUMBERS, so at-or-above-one-hundred means the lane is completely spent; there is no band between ample and gone. The live reading that exposed it: one endpoint reported ninety-seven percent used and three percent remaining on a three-hundred-minute window, and the view reported that it will serve. By the time that guard can fire, a dispatch has already been refused. This is the same shape as a guard that reports safety it does not provide, and this project has shipped one before: a state that could not fire at any input in its own domain, past a clean gate, because its falsifier ranged over the live inventory rather than over the input range. AND THE READING'S AGE IS IGNORED. That ninety-seven percent observation was fifty-five minutes old when the view served it, on a window that resets in hours, and the row carried the observation time without letting it qualify the claim. A lane's utilisation at some point in the past does not support a statement about whether it will serve now; the older the reading, the less it supports, and a reading old enough supports nothing. The view already carries the observation time on every row, so the input exists and is simply unused. WHAT TO CHANGE. Give the serving state at least three outcomes: one for a lane whose measured utilisation leaves clear room, one for a lane close enough to its ceiling that a dispatch is at risk, and one for a lane whose reading is too old to support a claim about the present. Name them by what the reader should conclude, not by a number. Declare the utilisation band and the staleness horizon as named module constants with a comment giving the reason for each value, and choose values you can justify in that comment rather than round numbers: the utilisation figure is quantised to whole percent, so a band narrower than a few points is measuring quantisation, and the staleness horizon must be short relative to the shortest window the view reports, which is three hundred minutes. Keep the exhausted outcome for a lane at its ceiling. A lane whose reading is stale must not be reported as ample even when the stale figure was low, because that is the direction that costs a refused dispatch; equally it must not be reported as exhausted, because that would hold work for no reason, and the honest third state is what avoids choosing between two wrong answers. FIX THE TWO ABSENCE DEFECTS IN THE SAME NODE, since both are the same error and both were asked for and not delivered. First, a lane that writes no receipt of this kind because it is not metered through this mechanism is a DIFFERENT state from a lane whose receipt should exist and is missing, and the view currently reports both as unreadable with the same reason. Distinguish them: several lanes in the live output are unmetered through this surface by nature and will never have a receipt, and reporting them as unreadable invites a reader to think something is broken. Second, a lane whose receipt is missing carries an observation time anyway, in one live case two days old, which is some other quantity presented in the field a reader will take as the receipt's observation time. When there is no receipt there is no observation, so that field must say so rather than carry a timestamp from elsewhere; if the timestamp is genuinely useful, give it a name that says what it measures. WHAT NOT TO DO. Do not add a recommendation, a ranking, or a preferred lane; the existing test that scans the response for such a field must keep passing, and this node must not weaken it. Do not compute a burn rate or project a reset. Do not change the quota readings themselves, the horizon keying, the effective context window or the plan type. Do not edit reckon/crew/rollout.py, reckon/crew/recovery.py, reckon/crew/ticker.py, reckon/crew/promotion.py, reckon/ledger.py, reckon/crew/quota_weight.py or reckon/schema/flight.yaml; peers hold all seven. Do not edit any file outside the repository, and in particular do not touch the host flight configuration even though it still declares a withdrawn lane; that is the coordinator's to raise. FALSIFIERS, in tests/test_lanes_view_serving_state.py, every fixture synthesised, no test reading the real configuration home or a real session file, and every expected figure computed in the test from the declared constants rather than written as a literal. RANGE THE UTILISATION FALSIFIER OVER THE INPUT RANGE, NOT OVER THE LANES THAT HAPPEN TO EXIST: assert the state at a sweep of utilisation values from zero to one hundred inclusive, including every value in the at-risk band and the values immediately either side of its boundary, and require the boundary to fall exactly where the constant declares. A fixture at ninety-seven percent on a fresh reading does NOT report the ample state, asserted directly against the ample state's own value, which is the live case that exposed this. A fixture at the ceiling still reports exhausted. A fixture whose reading is older than the staleness horizon reports the stale state regardless of how low its utilisation is, asserted with a deliberately low utilisation so a lenient implementation cannot pass. A fixture one second inside the horizon reports on its utilisation, pinning the boundary both ways. A lane unmetered through this surface reports its own state, distinguishable from a lane whose receipt is missing, asserted against each other directly. A lane with no receipt reports no observation time rather than a timestamp, asserted by requiring the field to be the unmeasured marker. Every existing lanes-view test passes unchanged. Report base and head over tests/test_lanes_view_serving_state.py, tests/test_crew_lanes_view.py and the tests importing reckon.mcp_views, with failure ids either side and none added. Bound the run per file and never run the full suite.

node_definition.done_when: pytest tests/test_promotion_harvests_the_receipt.py -q passes, and promoting a run on a metered lane attaches that lane's quota reading, harvested by the harness from the client's own per-session receipt, to both the promotion result the orchestrator reads and the committed ledger row, marking an unmetered or unreadable lane as unmeasured rather than as zero. WHY THIS SHAPE AND NOT A POLL. An orchestrator needs to know which lanes will serve its next dispatch. A poll has to guess when to look and is stale the moment it returns. A terminal run already holds a first-party reading of exactly the lane it just consumed, taken at the instant it stopped consuming it, and the orchestrator is already reading at that moment because promotion is a beat it cannot skip. So the freshest available reading rides along at no extra call. Two consequences beyond convenience. The quota field is reported in whole numbers, so no single reading can attribute one run's cost, but every terminal run stamps one reading with its own observation time, and many readings across a day recover a per-lane burn rate that no individual reading could; today's fleet would already have produced about twenty. And the availability surface being built alongside this can then read the most recent terminal reading per lane and say how old it is, instead of hunting session files. THE HARNESS HARVESTS IT; THE WORKER MUST NOT REPORT IT. This is the load-bearing constraint and it is not negotiable. Read the receipt in the promotion code path, from the client's own file, keyed by the run's recorded session id. Do not add a manifest field for it, do not read it from anything the worker wrote, and do not ask a worker for it. A metric a worker states about its own run stops being independent evidence of that run: this project has measured a brief that merely named a signature contaminating every stream in a wave and the verification along with it. State that reason in a comment at the harvest site, because the next reader will otherwise think a manifest field would have been simpler. WHERE TO GET IT. Read through reckon.crew.rollout, which already locates a session's receipt by its session id and already returns quota readings keyed by the length of the window they describe, with a weekly accessor and a short-horizon accessor. Attach every horizon the receipt reports, each with its window length, its utilisation, its reset time and the time the reading was observed. Do not select one horizon and do not reduce them to a worst case: they are separate budgets with different reset times, measured four hours apart on one account today, and an orchestrator needs each. Also attach the effective context window the receipt reports, which varies by lane by a factor of two and is the best single predictor of whether a node fits. THREE STATES THAT MUST NOT COLLAPSE. A lane that reports no quota because it is unmetered, a lane whose receipt could not be read, and a lane whose window genuinely reads zero used are three different facts. Mark the first two unmeasured, each distinguishably, and keep a measured zero as zero. This project already nulls and flags an unmetered lane's cost rather than recording it as free, precisely so a free lane cannot rank as the cheapest on a surface that sorts by cost; follow that precedent rather than inventing a second convention. WHAT NOT TO DO. Do not make promotion fail, refuse or warn because a receipt is missing: promotion's job is unchanged and an absent reading is a normal outcome for an unmetered lane. Do not compute headroom, a verdict, an availability judgement or a burn rate here; this attaches a reading. Do not touch reckon/crew/quota_weight.py, reckon/_flight_schema.py, reckon/_mcp_tools.py, reckon/mcp_views.py, reckon/mcp.py or reckon/crew/rollout.py; peers hold the first two and the middle three, and the last is the module you consume rather than change. Add the new record key to the ledger's declared record fields, since a tuple there is now held complete by a test and a key written without being declared is the drift that test exists to catch. FALSIFIERS, in tests/test_promotion_harvests_the_receipt.py, using the project's existing promotion test fixtures and a synthesised temporary repository, never a real checkout and never the real configuration home or live-pointer directory. A promotion of a run whose fixture receipt reports two horizons attaches both, each identifiable by its window length, and the shorter horizon's utilisation never appears as the longer one's, asserted against the longer one's value directly. The attached reading appears on BOTH the promotion result and the committed ledger row, asserted separately, because one without the other is the half-delivery this project has repeatedly measured: a capability that lands in the module owning the mechanism while the surface a reader reaches stays unchanged. A promotion of a run on a lane whose fixture declares it unmetered attaches an unmeasured marker and not a zero, asserted against a fixture whose measured utilisation is genuinely zero so the two cannot compare equal. A promotion whose receipt is absent attaches the unmeasured marker, distinguishably from the unmetered case, and the promotion still succeeds with its existing result unchanged in every other respect. The attached reading carries an observation time. Every existing promotion test passes with its assertions unchanged, which is the pin on promotion's unchanged behaviour, and the record-field completeness test passes with the new key declared. Report base and head over tests/test_promotion_harvests_the_receipt.py, the existing promotion tests, and the record-field completeness test, with failure ids either side and none added. Bound the run per file and never run the full suite.

node_definition.done_when: pytest tests/test_quota_weight.py -q passes, tests/test_skill_contracts.py reports no failure attributable to reckon/crew/quota_weight.py, and that module names no concrete model identifier and encodes no relative ordering between named models; the rates it applies arrive from configuration instead. THE VIOLATION, and it is the coordinator's doing. reckon/crew/quota_weight.py lines 17 to 19 declare three module constants binding a concrete model identifier each, and their names encode a hierarchy between them: one is the reference, one the middle, one the efficient member. A repository contract test fails on this, and the binding rule behind that test is that source, plans, skills and schemas may record task requirements and validation floors but must not prescribe concrete models, model families, or relative model hierarchies. A worker on an unrelated documentation node found the red test, correctly declined to fix it outside its scope, and reported it. The earlier brief for that module asked for exactly this shape, so the module did what it was told and the contract is what was wrong with the instruction. WHY THE RULE IS RIGHT HERE AND NOT MERELY A LINT. Two independent reasons, both of which this module already violates in substance. A rate is a moving number, and a moving number written into source is a fuse: when the vendor reprices, the module lies with no code change and no test failure. And a hierarchy in source makes the code the authority on which lane is stronger, which is a policy question the operator owns and which the surrounding design has deliberately refused to answer anywhere else — every other component built today reports and declines to rank. WHAT TO CHANGE. Take the rate table from the project's flight configuration through the existing flight reader rather than from module constants, so a lane's rate lives beside that lane's other declarations and a repricing is a configuration edit. Read the rates for the backends configuration declares; where a backend declares no rate, that backend must return the existing explicit unknown, which is the behaviour the module already has for an unrecognised identifier and which must be preserved exactly. Remove the three constants and every name that encodes a position in a hierarchy. Choose a reference for the dimensionless ratio without naming a model in source: derive it from the configuration itself, and state in a comment how the reference is chosen and why the choice cannot be a model name. If the configuration declares no rates at all, every lookup returns the unknown and nothing raises; a module that cannot price anything must say so rather than fall back to a table. ADD THE RATES TO CONFIGURATION AS PART OF THIS NODE, in the flight configuration schema and its declared defaults inside the repository, never in any file outside it: you must not edit anything under the user's home configuration directory. Put the per-million input and output rates alongside each backend's existing declaration in the repository's own schema and example or default configuration, so the shape is documented where a reader configuring a lane will meet it. The three rates currently in the module are the ones to carry across; take them from the module as it stands rather than from any other source, because preserving today's numbers exactly is what makes this a refactor whose behaviour a test can pin. WHAT NOT TO DO. Do not change the weighting arithmetic, the surcharge rule, the threshold constant, the per-request signature, the unknown behaviour, or the zero and negative handling: all six landed correctly an hour ago and are pinned by existing tests that must keep passing unchanged. Do not add a lane ranking, a recommendation or a default rate. Do not touch reckon/crew/lane_evidence.py, which imports this module and whose peer is finished but whose tests must keep passing, and do not touch reckon/crew/promotion.py, reckon/_mcp_tools.py, reckon/mcp_views.py, reckon/mcp.py or reckon/crew/dispatch.py; peers hold or recently held those. FALSIFIERS, in tests/test_quota_weight.py, every expected figure computed in the test from the configured rates rather than written as a literal. Every existing test in that file still passes with its assertions unchanged in meaning, which is the pin on the arithmetic; where a test previously imported a model constant, it now obtains that identifier from a test fixture configuration instead. Grep the module's own source text in a test and assert it contains no string matching a concrete model identifier and no identifier whose name encodes a hierarchy position, so the violation cannot return; state in the test docstring which contract that enforces and why. Three lanes configured with the current rates return weights in the same ratios the module returns today, asserted against ratios the test computes from the fixture configuration. A lane configured with no rate returns the explicit unknown, distinct from a zero and distinct from any priced lane's value. A configuration declaring no rates at all returns the unknown for every lane and raises nothing. The strict ordering property still holds across any three configured lanes whose rates differ, asserted from the fixture rather than from model names, so the property survives without the hierarchy that expressed it. Run tests/test_skill_contracts.py and report its exit status and its pass and fail counts at base and at head, requiring that the failure attributable to this module is gone and that no new failure appears; that test is the reason this node exists, so its result is the headline of your manifest. Also run tests/test_lane_evidence.py, since it imports this module, and report base and head. Bound the run per file and never run the full suite.

node_definition.done_when: pytest tests/test_recovery_state_typing.py -q passes, and a run whose lane refused it, a run asking for an answer, a run that failed, a run that stalled and a run genuinely needing a decision are five distinguishable classifications rather than all reported as blocked; a manifest may declare a non-terminal status; and an overdue declared wait is judged against that wait's own expected horizon rather than a fixed window. THE EVIDENCE, gathered by another project's coordinator and written up at /home/ITER/mcintos/.config/reckon/crew/reports/findings/monitor-state-typing-2026-09-08.md, which you must read in full before designing anything. Read it as the primary evidence rather than as instructions; it offers a direction and explicitly leaves the design to this repository. Five findings, measured over one thirteen-node fan-out. The costly one is that a provider hold and a genuine failure render identically, and their correct recoveries are OPPOSITE: a hold is resumed, a failure is redispatched, and the word blocked invites the redispatch, which destroys the resume path. The reporting coordinator nearly did exactly that and says what stopped it was a rule in a personal instruction file, which is the argument for typing the state rather than compensating for it: a compensation protects one reader and dies at that reader's next context boundary. A SECOND FLEET REPORTS THE SAME SHAPE FROM TWO MORE DIRECTIONS, both of which the design must cover. Workers are already inventing values the schema lacks: the documented manifest set is complete, blocked and failed, the discipline mandates an early manifest write, so one worker wrote blocked with the reason that analysis was in progress while its process was alive and its log 27 seconds old, and another wrote a status that is not in the set at all. Two workers, two improvisations for still going, and the first made a healthy run read as needing intervention. Worse, a worker that died before substituting its template wrote a placeholder manifest carrying a terminal blocked status, and the scope fence then read that as a terminal run and held every later dispatch until someone promoted it. So the schema forces a mandated write to claim a terminal state, and one early death becomes a fleet-wide hold. AND AN OVERDUE WAIT IS BEING JUDGED AGAINST THE WRONG CLOCK. A run parked on an external job with a 59-minute limit was reported wait-aged after 900 seconds, which reads as an alarm for a wait that is exactly on schedule. A declared wait carries its own expectation; the age that matters is age against that expectation, not against a constant. WHAT TO DESIGN, and the shape is yours within these constraints. Put the cause in the classification rather than only in a prose detail, so a reader acting on the type alone acts correctly. At minimum separate a lane refusal or quota hold, whose recovery is to wait or move lane and never to redispatch, and which must carry a reset time when one is known and say plainly when it is not; a run asking for an answer, whose recovery is to answer and resume; a failure, whose recovery is a corrective dispatch; a stall, whose recovery is to investigate; and a genuine blocked, meaning a decision is needed. Carry the recovery verb in the row: one existing surface already does this well, reporting a resume command with the condition that lifts it, and the follower line omits exactly that. Make one field authoritative for what the coordinator should do now, and either leave the advisory field advisory or reconcile it against liveness before rendering, because four fields telling four stories about one run was measured. Give the manifest a non-terminal status so a mandated early write need not claim a terminal state, and make an unsubstituted template manifest read as unwritten rather than as terminal. Judge an overdue declared wait against the horizon that wait declares. PRESERVE WHAT ALREADY WORKS, and it is written into the module: the existing comment distinguishing the stop that lifts itself from the stop that demands a reader is the correct principle and your vocabulary must keep it, including the requirement that a self-lifting state always names what will lift it so it never becomes the bucket a forgotten run sits in. Keep every existing classification that still means something and do not rename one whose meaning you are not changing. WHAT NOT TO DO. Do not change the resume gate's budget reading in this node: that is the reported finding about two surfaces disagreeing at one instant, it needs the lane probe, and it is a separate node. Do not touch reckon/crew/promotion.py, reckon/ledger.py, reckon/crew/quota_weight.py, reckon/crew/lane_evidence.py, reckon/_mcp_tools.py, reckon/mcp_views.py, reckon/mcp.py, reckon/schema/flight.yaml or reckon/crew/dispatch.py; peers hold or recently held all nine. Do not add a state whose recovery is the same as an existing state's; a distinction that changes no action is noise. FALSIFIERS, in tests/test_recovery_state_typing.py, every fixture synthesised and never reading the real configuration home or live-pointer directory. A fixture run refused by its lane classifies distinguishably from a fixture run that failed, asserted directly against each other, and the refused one's recovery text names resuming while the failed one's does not name resuming, so the two opposite recoveries cannot be confused by a reader following the type. A refused run with a known reset time carries it; one without says so explicitly rather than omitting the field. A fixture manifest declaring a non-terminal status with a live process and a fresh log does NOT classify as blocked, which is the healthy-run-reads-as-actionable case. A template manifest whose placeholders are unsubstituted classifies as unwritten and NOT as terminal, and a test asserts it does not satisfy whatever predicate the scope fence uses for terminality, so one early death cannot hold a fleet. A declared wait with a long horizon is not overdue at an age that would be overdue for a short one, asserted by two fixtures differing only in their declared horizon, which is the property a fixed window cannot express. Every row carrying an actionable classification also carries a recovery verb, asserted over the whole vocabulary by iterating it rather than by naming states one at a time, so a future state cannot be added without one. The self-lifting states each name what lifts them, asserted the same way. Every existing recovery test passes with its assertions unchanged in meaning. Report base and head over tests/test_recovery_state_typing.py, the existing recovery and ticker tests, and the crew tests, with failure ids either side and none added. Bound the run per file and never run the full suite.

node_definition.done_when: pytest tests/test_lane_change_reads_the_worktree.py -q passes, and the prompt a redispatched worker receives states the inherited worktree's actual state, read at the moment the prompt is composed rather than described by the coordinator from an earlier reading. THE DEFECT AND THE MEASURED COST, reported by another fleet's coordinator today. reckon/crew/dispatch.py composes the fresh-start prompt in _lane_prompt around line 3063: it reads the original prompt from disk, appends a lane-changed notice, the reason and the coordinator's advice, and stops. Nothing in it reads the worktree the new worker is about to inherit. So the only account of that worktree is whatever the coordinator wrote into the advice, from a reading taken before the outgoing worker was stopped. Measured: a coordinator's advice said the inherited worktree carried no modifications, the outgoing worker made its first and only edit, a single import line, in the seconds between that reading and the stop, and the incoming worker refused to start on an unexpected pre-existing modification to an assigned path. The handoff went stale inside the window the procedure itself creates, and no amount of coordinator care closes that window, because the reading and the stop cannot be simultaneous. A SECOND MEASURED CASE MAKES THE SAME POINT FROM THE OTHER SIDE, and it is the more expensive one. A worker was killed at its harness ceiling while an external compute job it had submitted kept running; the recoverable fact was a live job owned by a dead run, and it existed only as prose in the dead worker's manifest. A redispatch onto another lane recovered it, but only because the coordinator happened to put the job id into the advice by hand. The general shape of both cases is the same: the successor is told about its inheritance by a human intermediary rather than by a reading, and everything the intermediary omits or misremembers is lost. WHAT TO CHANGE. When composing a fresh-start prompt for a lane change, read the inherited worktree at that moment and state what is there: the porcelain status and a per-file change summary, and the head commit the worktree sits on together with whether that commit differs from the run's recorded base. Put it in the prompt as a stated fact rather than as advice, clearly separated from the coordinator's own advice so the worker can tell a reading from an instruction, and label it with the time it was taken. Keep the coordinator's advice exactly as it is passed; this adds a reading, it does not replace or edit what the coordinator wrote. When the porcelain status returns no entries, say that explicitly rather than omitting the section, because an absent section is indistinguishable from a section nobody generated. ALSO SURFACE THE UNCOMMITTED WORK AS THE EXPOSURE IT IS. Where the reading shows uncommitted changes, the prompt must instruct the successor to commit them as a checkpoint before continuing, and say why in one clause: an inherited diff is the only copy of that work and a later refusal or death takes it. That instruction has been given by hand by two coordinators today and worked both times; putting it in the composed prompt is what stops it depending on either of them remembering. WHAT NOT TO DO. Do not read or run anything outside the inherited worktree, and do not attempt to discover external compute jobs in this node; the abandoned-run job-recovery case belongs to a separate node in the classification module, which a peer holds. Do not change the same-session advice path, which passes the coordinator's advice through unchanged and must keep doing so. Do not change what the lane change does to the run record, the backend resolution, or the retained worktree itself. Do not edit reckon/crew/recovery.py, reckon/crew/ticker.py, reckon/mcp_views.py, reckon/crew/quota_weight.py, reckon/schema/flight.yaml or reckon/ledger.py; peers hold all six. Do not fail a lane change because the worktree cannot be read: state that it could not be read, and why, and continue, because refusing to hand off a run whose worktree is unreadable strands it exactly where the old behaviour stranded it. FALSIFIERS, in tests/test_lane_change_reads_the_worktree.py, using a synthesised temporary git repository as the inherited worktree, never a real checkout and never the real configuration home. A fresh-start prompt composed against a worktree carrying an uncommitted modification contains that file's path, and contains the checkpoint instruction; assert both, and assert the path appears even when the coordinator's advice is empty, which is the case the coordinator cannot cover by hand. A prompt composed against a worktree whose porcelain status returns no entries contains an affirmative statement to that effect, asserted by looking for that statement rather than by asserting the absence of a path. The coordinator's advice text appears in the prompt unchanged, byte for byte, alongside the reading, asserted with an advice string containing text that would be damaged by any rewriting. THE READING AND THE ADVICE ARE DISTINGUISHABLE IN THE PROMPT, asserted by requiring a labelled boundary between them, because a worker that cannot tell a measurement from an instruction will treat one as the other. The reading carries the time it was taken. A worktree whose head differs from the run's recorded base reports both, asserted with a fixture where they differ. A worktree that cannot be read yields a prompt saying so and does not raise, asserted by pointing the record at a path that does not exist. The same-session advice path is unchanged, asserted by composing one and requiring it to equal what it produces today. Report base and head over the new test file and the tests importing reckon.crew.dispatch, with failure ids either side and none added. Bound the run per file and never run the full suite.

node_definition.done_when: pytest tests/test_promotion_beat_carries_fleet_state.py -q passes, and the result a promotion returns carries a short fleet-state reading beside the quota reading it already carries, so an orchestrator's picture of its own fleet is refreshed at every landing without a separate read. WHY THIS COMPLETES A HALF-BUILT DESIGN. Promotion already attaches a lane quota reading harvested from the client's own receipt, and that half works: the newest promoted row carries quota_state, an observation time, the effective context window and the quota windows keyed by length. What it does not carry is anything about the FLEET, and the fleet is what the orchestrator is about to make its next decision about. So a coordinator that has just landed a node still has to issue a separate read to learn whether anything else is live, whether a run is unreconciled, whether a lane is occupied, or whether a followup is waiting — at exactly the moment it is already reading a result. The promotion beat is the one moment an orchestrator cannot skip, which is why the reading belongs there rather than on a schedule. WHAT TO ATTACH, and the constraint that matters most is BREVITY. This is a beat, not a report: a handful of scalars an orchestrator can act on without parsing. Include the number of runs still live in this project, the number that are unreconciled, the count of runs whose classification is actionable together with the classifications present, and the number of distinct lanes currently occupied. Include the fleet observation time. Do not attach per-run rows, worktree paths, manifest digests, follower registrations or anything that grows with fleet size: a beat that grows unboundedly stops being read, and every one of those is already available from the views that exist for them. If you find yourself attaching a list whose length is the number of runs, stop and attach its count instead. DERIVE IT, DO NOT RECOMPUTE IT. The counts above are already derived by the existing live-pointer and drain reads; call those rather than reimplementing their logic, so the beat and the views cannot drift into disagreeing about one fleet. That is the whole point of putting the derivation in one place, and a second implementation of a count is the defect this project has repeatedly measured. THREE RULES. The beat is a reading and carries its own observation time, separate from the quota reading's, because the two are taken from different sources and one being fresh says nothing about the other. The beat never fails a promotion: if the fleet state cannot be read, attach an explicit unmeasured marker saying so and let the promotion succeed unchanged, exactly as the quota reading already degrades. And the beat states facts and recommends nothing: no readiness verdict, no next-node suggestion, no capacity judgement, because the orchestrator owns that decision and every other surface built here refuses to make it. Say that in a comment at the composition site. WHAT NOT TO TOUCH. Do not change what promotion does to the run record, the gate, the commit list, the suite delta or the lane quota receipt. Do not add the beat to the ledger row: the ledger is a durable record of one run and a fleet snapshot at that moment does not describe that run, so this belongs on the returned RESULT only, and a test must assert the ledger row is unchanged by it. Do not edit reckon/mcp_views.py, reckon/_backends.py, reckon/crew/recovery.py, reckon/crew/ticker.py or reckon/crew/rollout.py; a peer holds the first two and the rest are settled. FALSIFIERS, in tests/test_promotion_beat_carries_fleet_state.py, using the project's existing promotion fixtures and a synthesised temporary repository, never a real checkout and never the real configuration home or live-pointer directory. A promotion whose fixture fleet holds several live runs returns a beat whose live count equals the number the test constructed, and the same for the unreconciled count and the occupied-lane count, each asserted against a figure the test computes rather than a literal. The beat carries its own observation time, distinct from the quota reading's, asserted by constructing the two at different times and requiring both to appear. THE BEAT IS BOUNDED: assert that its size does not grow with fleet size, by composing it against a fixture with one live run and against one with many and requiring the same set of keys and no list whose length differs; that is the assertion that keeps it a beat. A fixture whose fleet state cannot be read yields the unmeasured marker and a promotion that still succeeds with its other fields unchanged. The committed ledger row is byte-identical with and without the beat, asserted directly, so the durable record is untouched. The beat contains no field naming a recommended, preferred, ready or suggested next action, asserted by scanning its keys and values, pinning the no-recommendation rule the way the lanes view already pins it. Every existing promotion test passes with its assertions unchanged. Report base and head over the new file and the existing promotion tests, with failure ids either side and none added. Bound the run per file and never run the full suite.

node_definition.done_when: pytest tests/test_lanes_view_is_live.py -q passes, and the lanes view never reports a quota reading as too old to use: it obtains a live reading by probing, and where a probe cannot describe a particular lane's own quota it falls back to that lane's own most recent receipt and names which source answered. WHY THE CURRENT BEHAVIOUR IS WRONG. The view was given a stale state an hour ago because its only input was a per-session receipt file that ages, and reporting an old reading as current would have been worse. That was the right call for the inputs it had and the wrong design for the tool: this surface exists so an orchestrator can ask whether a lane will serve before dispatching, and answering that it does not know is a refusal to do its one job when the means to answer exist. A live probe exists in this repository and the view does not use it. WHAT THE PROBE IS, so you do not have to find it. reckon/_backends.py defines budget_probe for the metered dialect: it launches the harness command's app-server transport and issues an initialize handshake followed by an account rate-limits read, and that read RUNS NO MODEL, so it costs no quota and no tokens. Its answer carries used percentages and reset times for SEVERAL metered windows at once. read_probe currently reduces that answer to a single window, choosing whichever is furthest through. The probe machinery, its caching field and a cache lifetime in the budget policy all already exist; what is missing is the lanes view consulting it. THE ROOT DEFECT THE PROBE ALONE DOES NOT FIX, and this is the part to get right. The probe is keyed to the harness COMMAND, and four configured lanes share one command, so a single account reading is currently attributed to four lanes whose quotas differ. Measured on this host: the budget surface reports all four at an identical utilisation and an identical burn multiple, while one of those lanes has its own separate quota entirely, sitting at 97 percent of a five-hour window and 43 percent of a weekly window that resets about 3.7 hours later than the shared one. So a probe used naively would still describe that lane with another lane's figure, and it would do so with the authority of a fresh reading, which is worse than a stale one. WHAT TO BUILD. Probe for a live reading when composing the view. Key every window the probe returns by its own window_minutes rather than reducing to one, the way the receipt reader already does, and expose each. For every lane, decide which source describes THAT lane and say so on the row: a probe reading whose windows match the lane's own quota structure, or that lane's own most recent receipt where the probe cannot distinguish it. Carry the source name and the observation time on every reading, so a reader can see whether it came from a live probe or from a receipt, and never present a receipt figure as a probe reading. Keep the at-risk band and the exhausted state exactly as they are. Retire the stale state ONLY for lanes the probe can describe; a lane whose only available evidence is an old receipt must still say so rather than pretend, because inventing currency is the failure this whole surface exists to prevent — the honest form is a fresh-probe row for lanes the probe covers and a receipt-sourced row, with its age, for lanes it does not. DO NOT MAKE THE VIEW SLOW OR FRAGILE. Use the existing cache lifetime rather than a new one, so repeated reads in a short window do not relaunch the probe. A probe that fails, times out or is unavailable must degrade to the receipt path and say that the probe did not answer, never raise and never block the view; a view that cannot be read is worse than one reading from a receipt. Do not probe a lane whose dialect declares no probe. Do not run any model, and do not add a second probe implementation: use budget_probe and read_probe, extending read_probe to keep every window rather than reducing to one if that is what keying requires. WHAT NOT TO TOUCH. Do not change budget admission in this node even though it has the same attribution defect; that is a separate node with a refusal path attached and a followup already recording it. Do not edit reckon/crew/rollout.py, reckon/crew/recovery.py, reckon/crew/ticker.py, reckon/crew/promotion.py or reckon/ledger.py. FALSIFIERS, in tests/test_lanes_view_is_live.py, every probe stubbed rather than launched, no test running a real command, reading the real configuration home or touching a real session file. A lane the stub probe describes reports a probe-sourced reading with the probe's observation time, and does NOT report the stale state even when a receipt for that lane is hours old, asserted with a deliberately ancient receipt present so a lenient implementation cannot pass. A stub probe returning two windows of different lengths yields two readings keyed by their lengths, and the shorter window's utilisation never appears as the longer one's, asserted against the longer one's value directly. A lane whose quota the probe cannot describe reports its receipt as the source, with an age, and is distinguishable from a probe-sourced row by the source field alone. A stub probe that raises, and one that returns nothing, both degrade to the receipt path, say the probe did not answer, and do not raise. Two reads inside the cache lifetime launch the probe once, asserted by counting stub invocations. A lane whose dialect declares no probe is never probed, asserted the same way. The at-risk band and the exhausted state return exactly what they return today for the same utilisations, asserted against figures the test computes from the declared constants. And the existing no-recommendation test still passes unchanged. Report base and head over the new file, tests/test_lanes_view_serving_state.py, tests/test_crew_lanes_view.py and the tests importing reckon.mcp_views, with failure ids either side and none added. Bound the run per file and never run the full suite.

node_definition.done_when: A report file exists at the declared write path stating whether this worker could call the imas-dd MCP server from inside its own dispatched process, naming the tool it called, the version range that tool returned, and the verbatim error if it could not. WHY THIS IS WORTH A NODE AND WHY YOU ARE THE RIGHT PROCESS TO RUN IT. Dispatch here is command-line led: the coordinator launches a separate harness process, so whatever tools THAT harness has are what a worker has, and they are not the coordinator's tools. The coordinator can call an MCP server and learn nothing about you. Only a call made inside your own process settles it. The host configuration declares three MCP servers to your harness — one served over HTTP at an ITER address, one launched as a local module, one launched through a project runner — and nobody has ever confirmed that a non-interactive dispatched run reaches any of them. If it does, briefs across this fleet can start naming authoritative lookups instead of asking workers to infer facts. If it does not, that is equally valuable and must be recorded as plainly. WHAT TO DO. Attempt to call the imas-dd MCP server for the range of IMAS data-dictionary versions it knows about — the earliest and the latest, and however it expresses the set between them. Use whatever tool that server exposes for listing or describing versions; discover the tool from the server rather than assuming a name, and record the exact tool name you called. Then write the report. THE REPORT MUST DISTINGUISH FOUR OUTCOMES, and stating which one occurred is the deliverable. The server answered and you have a version range. The server was reachable but the call was refused or errored, in which case give the verbatim error. The tools were not present in your process at all, meaning the harness exposed no MCP surface to this run. Or the attempt could not be made for some other reason you name. Do not collapse any of these into another, and do not report an inability as a version range. THE ANTI-FABRICATION RULE IS THE POINT OF THE WHOLE NODE. You may know something about IMAS data-dictionary versions from training, and a plausible answer from memory would be indistinguishable in the report from a real tool result while being worthless as evidence about tool access. So the report must carry, for the successful case, the tool name you called and the response as the tool returned it, and must state explicitly that the figures came from that call. If you cannot call a tool, you must NOT supply a version range from any other source — not from memory, not from a file on disk, not from a web page. Say the call failed and give the error. A report containing a version range without a tool name and a tool response is a failed node regardless of whether the numbers are correct. Do not read any repository file, environment variable or configuration file to answer the version question: the question is whether the TOOL answers, and any other route defeats it. WHAT ELSE TO RECORD, because it costs you nothing and answers the next question. List every MCP tool name visible in your process, if any are, so the fleet learns what a dispatched worker actually has rather than what the configuration declares. If the list is empty, say so as a list of length zero rather than as prose. Note whether any call required an approval you could not give, since one server is configured with an approval mode and a non-interactive process cannot answer a prompt — that specific outcome, a tool present but unusable without an approver, is the one most likely to be misread as absence, so name it if you meet it. WHAT NOT TO DO. Write nothing outside the declared write path. Do not install, start, configure or edit any MCP server, and do not edit any configuration file. Do not attempt to work around a failure by calling the server over plain HTTP yourself: the question is what the harness gives you, and a manual request answers a different one. Do not run the repository's test suite; this node has no code gate. FALSIFIERS. The report exists at the declared path and names exactly one of the four outcomes. For the successful case it carries the tool name, the tool's own response, and the earliest and latest versions read from that response. For any unsuccessful case it carries the verbatim error text or the empty tool list. The report states the harness and model it was produced by, taken from your own runtime rather than from the brief, so a later reader can tell which lane was tested. The report contains no version figure that is not attributable to a named tool response, which you confirm by rereading your own report before finishing and saying in the manifest that you did. State in the manifest the count of MCP tools you could see.

node_definition.done_when: pytest tests/test_mcp_tool_names_are_regular.py -q passes, and every tool the reckon MCP server publishes carries an explicit wire name with no leading underscore, so each is addressed as mcp followed by the server name, a double separator, and the tool name, exactly as the other servers on this workstation are. THE DEFECT, measured from inside two dispatched worker processes today. The server registers five tools with a FastMCP decorator applied to module-private functions named with a leading underscore, and FastMCP takes the wire name from the function name. So the underscore that marks a function private in Python leaks into the published name and absorbs a separator. Measured: three of the four MCP servers declared on this workstation publish as mcp, server, double separator, tool. Reckon alone publishes with a single separator on one host and with three underscores on another, for the same five tools. That is not cosmetic. A coordinator matching tool names by pattern found none of reckon's tools, concluded the server was unreachable from dispatched workers, reported that as a finding, and was wrong; the server was answering the whole time. The irregularity cost a false absence claim in a committed record. WHAT TO CHANGE. Give each of the five tool registrations an explicit published name equal to the function name with its leading underscore removed, so the five become the plain nouns and verbs they already are. Keep every Python function name exactly as it is: those underscores are correct, the functions are module-private, and renaming them would ripple through internal call sites for no benefit. The change is confined to the decorator call. Read the file to find all five rather than trusting a list, and say in your manifest how many you found, because a rename that misses one leaves the inconsistency it exists to remove. UPDATE THE HOST HARNESS CONFIGURATION IN THE SAME NODE, because two of the five are named there and would otherwise silently stop matching. The workstation configuration file for the metered harness declares per-tool approval settings keyed by the old names for two of these tools. Those keys must move to the new names. That file is outside the repository; you are permitted to edit ONLY those two keys in it and nothing else, and you must report the before and after of each line you touched verbatim in your manifest. Do not add, remove or reorder any other key, and do not touch any other file outside the repository. THIS IS A BREAKING CHANGE AND MUST BE STATED WHERE A CALLER WILL MEET IT. Any session holding a connection to this server keeps calling the old names until it reconnects, and will meet a tool-not-found. Record the old and new spelling for both host conventions in the repository's own documentation of this surface, so the next reader can map a stale call rather than guess. Find where this server's tools are already documented and put it there rather than creating a new file. WHAT NOT TO DO. Do not change any tool's arguments, behaviour, return shape or description. Do not add or remove a tool. Do not change the server's own name. Do not touch reckon/crew/recovery.py, reckon/mcp_views.py, reckon/crew/promotion.py or reckon/_backends.py. Do not restart or reconnect anything: the operator owns that beat and a worker cannot do it. FALSIFIERS, in tests/test_mcp_tool_names_are_regular.py. Instantiate or introspect the server and assert the published name of every registered tool, by iterating the registry rather than by naming the five, so a sixth tool added later is held to the same rule. Assert no published name begins with an underscore. Assert every published name matches the same shape as the others, stated as a pattern in the test with the contract named in its docstring. Assert the count of registered tools is unchanged from before your edit, computed in the test rather than written as a literal, so the rename cannot have dropped or added one. Assert each of the five publishes the exact expected plain name, derived in the test from the function names by stripping one leading underscore rather than hard-coded, so the test states the rule instead of restating the answer. Assert the Python function names still carry their leading underscore, which pins that only the wire name moved. And read the host configuration file back and assert the two approval keys carry the new names and that the file still parses, without asserting anything else about its contents. Report base and head over the new file and every test importing reckon.mcp, with failure ids either side and none added. Bound the run per file and never run the full suite.

node_definition.done_when: pytest tests/test_a_brief_points_rather_than_quotes.py -q passes, and a dispatch whose done-when reproduces a long contiguous span of its own plan section's text is reported at dispatch time with that span quoted back, so a coordinator sees it has copied the plan instead of pointing at it. WHY A CHECK AND NOT MORE GUIDANCE. The rule already exists, in writing, in this repository: skills/reckon-ship/references/sprint-orchestration.md says do not restate plan context, decisions, research or done-when criteria in the dispatch. Two coordinators broke it seven times between them today, and every one produced a defect. Mine, four: a done-when naming a discriminator the plan had already rejected, so the worker faced two contradictory authorities and changed nothing; a fence naming a generated file as the place to declare a configuration field; a fence excluding the test that imports the symbol the node had to remove; and an instruction to put values in a configuration layer whose own invariant forbids them. A peer's, three: a test list naming a file that exists only in a held prototype tree, an environment variable the production function does not honour, and a receipt path that had been re-keyed out from under the brief. In all seven the worker blocked or disputed and the change it named was the one that landed, while the coordinator's copy named a file, variable, path or measure that the source did not carry. So a written rule with no check decays exactly as this project has recorded elsewhere, and the remedy is a check bound to the moment that always happens. WHAT TO BUILD. At dispatch, after the node's plan and section are resolved and before the worker is launched, compare the done-when text against the text of that plan section. Where a contiguous run of the plan's own words reappears in the done-when beyond a declared length, report it: name the overlapping span, quote it, and say which plan section it came from. Put the report on the dispatch result so a coordinator reading the launch sees it, and record it on the run so a later reader can find it. Declare the length threshold as a named module constant with a comment justifying its value; choose it from what discriminates rather than from a round number, and say in the comment what a shorter span would catch that is legitimate. REPORT, DO NOT REFUSE, AND SAY WHY IN A COMMENT. A done-when legitimately shares short phrases with its plan: a file path, a function name, a measure's units, a threshold figure. Those are pointers, which is the behaviour the rule wants, and a refusal on them would make the check hated and then disabled. A long verbatim paragraph is a copy. The check therefore reports rather than blocks, and the report is the deliverable: a coordinator who sees its own copied paragraph quoted back will fix the brief, and one who is told a number is over a threshold will not. Do not add a flag to suppress it, and do not make it configurable off. NORMALISE BEFORE COMPARING, or the check is trivially defeated and worthless. The plan is HTML and the done-when is prose, so strip markup, collapse whitespace and compare on words rather than characters; a coordinator who reflows a copied paragraph has still copied it. Do not compare on a digest of the whole text, which changes with one word. Do not use a similarity score: a percentage cannot be quoted back to a reader, and quoting the span is the entire point. WHAT NOT TO TOUCH. Do not edit reckon/mcp.py, tests under it, or docs/AGENTS.md; a peer holds all three. Do not change the eight-property node contract, the existing dispatchability refusals, or any other validation. Do not read a plan from anywhere except the resolved plan the node already names, and do not fetch anything. FALSIFIERS, in tests/test_a_brief_points_rather_than_quotes.py, using the project's existing dispatch fixtures and a synthesised temporary repository, never a real checkout and never the real configuration home. A done-when carrying a long verbatim paragraph from its plan section produces a report naming the section and quoting the overlapping span, asserted by finding the span text inside the report rather than by asserting a boolean. THE GAP, measured by another fleet against the code this repository landed an hour ago. That change made a declared wait outrank worker liveness, and it holds for a wait whose external condition is still PENDING: one run with a waiting manifest, a dead process and a running job classifies as waiting and the sweep counts it. It fails for a wait whose condition is already MET: a sibling run with a waiting manifest, all five wait fields well-formed, a dead process and a job that COMPLETED in two minutes classifies as abandoned with the detail that the process is gone without a complete manifest, and the sweep does not count it at all. So the discriminator has moved one step rather than disappearing, and it now falls exactly on the case the sweep exists for — the job finished, so the run should resume, and instead it leaves the set that would have woken it. A coordinator recovered it by hand. WHY THE EXISTING FALSIFIER DID NOT CATCH IT, which is the lesson to encode rather than just the bug to fix. The landed test asserts one manifest fixture twice, differing only in process liveness, and requires the same classification both ways. That ranges over liveness and NOT over the wait's own condition state, so every fixture it uses has a pending condition and the met case cannot appear. The property under test is two-dimensional and the test covered one dimension. This project has now shipped this same shape three times: a guard whose falsifier ranged over the population where the failure could not occur. WHAT TO CHANGE. When a manifest declares a wait, read the declared condition's state before concluding anything from process liveness, and classify on the pair. A pending condition with a dead process stays waiting, which is today's behaviour and must not regress. A MET condition — the probe reporting one of the states the manifest's terminal list names — is a run whose wait is over and whose recovery is to resume; give it the classification whose recovery verb is resume, and make sure it is in whatever collection the resume sweep consumes. Do not invent a new classification if an existing one already carries the resume verb and the right meaning; the vocabulary landed with several, and adding a fourth word for a state one of them already names is noise. Keep the overdue-wait handling and the declared-horizon judgement exactly as they are. THE PROBE IS THE INPUT AND IT MUST NOT BE TRUSTED BLINDLY. The manifest carries the probe as an argv array and the terminal states as a list, so the condition's state is obtainable, but a probe can fail, time out, print nothing, or print something matching no terminal state. Each of those is UNKNOWN, not met and not unmet: a run whose probe cannot answer must stay waiting rather than become abandoned, because a probe failure says nothing about the worker and abandoned is the state this project reserves for proof of death. Say that in a comment. Do not let a probe failure block or slow the classifier: it must remain a cheap read that cannot fail, so bound the probe and degrade to waiting on any fault. node_definition.done_when: pytest tests/test_a_resume_does_not_inherit_its_baseline.py -q passes, and a resumed run's manifest is read rather than discarded, so a manifest a previous attempt wrote is no longer treated as absent by the attempt that inherited it. THE DEFECT, measured on a live peer fleet's runs at the current head with two adjacent fixes already merged. The classifier gates a manifest on freshness: the manifest must be newer than a baseline mtime recorded on the run. On a resumed run that baseline is captured from the manifest the PREVIOUS attempt wrote, so the inherited manifest's mtime equals the baseline exactly, is not newer, is judged stale, and is treated as absent. Measured on one run at attempt six: baseline 1788874593998173197 and manifest mtime 1788874593998173197, identical, and the tool reported no manifest status while the file plainly read status waiting with five well-formed wait fields. WHY IT IS WORSE THAN ONE MISREAD RUN. Across five live runs in that fleet, FOUR had their manifests discarded this way. One was a parked run whose file said waiting and which classified abandoned, left the collection the resume sweep walks, and sat wakeable and unwoken while its external job had already completed; a coordinator recovered it by hand. The other three had files saying failed or blocked and classified running, which is the same discard with an outcome that looks harmless and therefore went unnoticed in that coordinator's own table. So the defect is not that a parked run is misread. It is that A RESUMED RUN'S MANIFEST IS DISCARDED WHATEVER IT SAYS, and the parked case is merely where the fallback to process liveness is dangerous. Two earlier fixes for the parked symptom are already merged and neither can fire, because both require the classifier to see a declared wait and the manifest is discarded before the wait is read. WHAT TO CHANGE, AND WHAT NOT TO. Fix the baseline, not the gate. A resume must not adopt its predecessor's manifest as its own baseline: the baseline exists to answer whether THIS attempt has written anything, and an inherited manifest answers whether ANY attempt ever wrote anything, which is a different question and the wrong one. Exempting a waiting status from the freshness gate would leave that wrong answer in place everywhere else the baseline is consulted, and the three misclassified terminal rows above are that everywhere-else already visible. So do not special-case any status. THE BASELINE A RESUME MUST USE, stated rather than left to you: every attempt in one run's chain shares the baseline recorded at that run's FIRST dispatch, and a resume inherits that baseline value rather than recomputing one from its predecessor's manifest. Carry the original value forward on each resume. That serves both purposes at once and the comment must say so: a manifest written by ANY attempt of this run is newer than the first dispatch, so it is read whatever its status, which is the behaviour being restored; and a manifest predating the run entirely is still older than that baseline, so the gate keeps doing the one job it was built for. The distinction the gate was reaching for is not attempt-versus-attempt, it is this-run-versus-before-this-run, and a resume genuinely inherits its predecessor's manifest as a handover rather than meeting it as a stale artefact. Do not use the resume's own start time as the baseline: a parked run's manifest is written by the attempt that parked and therefore predates every later resume, so a start-time baseline discards exactly the case this node exists to fix. WHAT NOT TO TOUCH. Do not change the waiting classification, the met-wait condition handling, the recovery vocabulary or the resume sweep's membership: all three landed today and their tests must keep passing unchanged. Do not edit reckon/crew/promotion.py, reckon/mcp_views.py or reckon/crew/dispatch.py. Do not change what a worker writes or the manifest schema. FALSIFIERS, in tests/test_a_resume_does_not_inherit_its_baseline.py, every fixture synthesised, no test reading the real configuration home or live-pointer directory. RANGE OVER ATTEMPT NUMBER AND OVER MANIFEST STATUS AS A GRID, because the defect was found through one status and affects all of them: for a first attempt and for a resumed attempt, against manifest statuses of complete, blocked, failed and waiting, assert the manifest is READ in every cell, from one fixture varying only those two inputs. Eight cells, stated explicitly. A resumed run whose inherited manifest has an mtime exactly equal to the recorded baseline is read rather than discarded, asserted with the two values set equal, since equality rather than staleness is the measured trigger. The gate still does its original job: a manifest written BEFORE the current attempt began and carrying a terminal status from an earlier attempt is not credited to the current attempt as its outcome, asserted by a fixture where that distinction is the only difference, so the fix cannot be a blanket removal of the gate. A parked resumed run classifies into the waiting family and appears in the collection the resume sweep consumes, asserted by calling that path, which is the end-to-end statement of the recovered behaviour. The three terminal-status cases classify from their manifests rather than from process liveness. Every existing recovery, state-typing and met-wait test passes with its assertions unchanged. Report base and head over the new file, tests/test_recovery_state_typing.py, tests/test_a_met_wait_is_ready_not_abandoned.py and the recovery and resumption test files, with failure ids either side and none added. REPAIR THE FUNCTION, NOT A CALLER. dispatch.py:3840 _backend_settings returns {launch, command} from argv[0] the moment a recorded argv is present, BEFORE it consults config, discarding the window, the model and the effort. Make that branch merge: argv supplies the command, config supplies the rest, neither discards the other.

ONE CANDIDATE IS ALREADY DEAD - do not spend a measurement rediscovering it. Passing a config to _backend_settings from promotion.py:1483 changes nothing, because the argv branch returns first. Measured with a positive control: live pointers 37 of 37 carry top-level argv, ledger rows 0 of 977 do (977 cli rows). promotion.py:1483 reads the live pointer, so the short-circuit fires every time. The same short-circuit silently defeats the three dispatch.py callers at 3559, 3908 and 4194 that ALREADY pass a real config - repairing the function fixes those too, which is the larger half and is invisible from 1483. It also carries the fifth caller resumption.py:407 without editing it, which is why resumption.py is not in your write scope.

DONE WHEN, and every clause emits evidence:

(1) A backend rebuilt from a recorded argv resolves utilisation against the configured window. Assert through the dispatch path AND through promotion.py:1483, which feeds StreamMeasures and writes the promoted row's input_utilisation_pct. Both sites are in this one write scope and are asserted at the combined state; a worker asserting only its own half cannot see what the pair does. Report the test node ids and their pass count.

(2) An unresolvable window yields unknown utilisation, never an announced or constant fallback. Demonstrate this as a refusal - a test that fails if the code substitutes any figure - and report its node id.

(3) A resumed run carries its recorded model and effort: assert the mapping resume_plan hands launch_plan contains both, taken from the recorded argv rather than a provider default. Report the assertion and its result.

(4) A resumed run is context-checked or says so explicitly. _context_fit_verdict has exactly one call site, routing.py:1601, inside dispatch resolution; the resume path never reaches it. Prefer an explicit unchecked state reported from resume_plan. routing.py is NOT in your write scope - if you find routing genuinely required, block and say so rather than reaching outside the fence. Silence does not satisfy this clause: silence is indistinguishable from a check that passed.

(5) State as digits how many of the five _backend_settings callers lose a setting before the change and how many after. The second figure is zero.

A RECORDED ROW'S WINDOW IS NEVER RESOLVED BY LOOKUP. If you touch historical rows, take the window from that row's own agent.usable_input_window. Resolving an alias against current config is correct ONLY for a run being dispatched now. Measured: alias dsv4-flash carries true windows 1016576 AND 492288; dsv4.1-flash carries 172800 AND 1016576, because a row holds what was configured when it ran and the configuration has moved twice. An alias lookup gets exactly the nine understating rows wrong again, for a new reason. These are two different requirements and conflating them reintroduces the defect.

THE FALSIFIER RANGES OVER WINDOW SIZES, NOT JUST DIRECTIONS, AND NEVER OVER THE LIVE LANE INVENTORY. Census of 983 ledger rows: 125 divide by something other than the window recorded beside them - 111 at window 1016576 over divisor 200000 (overstates about fivefold), 5 more the same, 6 at window 172800 over divisor 200000 (UNDERSTATES), 3 at window 492288 over divisor 1016576 (UNDERSTATES about twofold). The worst understatement reports 81.9 percent where the true figure is 94.8. Understatement is the direction that admits a node which should be held, and it lands on the SMALLEST window in the fleet - unsafe exactly where headroom is scarcest and safe where it is plentiful. So carry at least one fixture window BELOW the divisor and one ABOVE, and report both results as numbers. A test asserting only that the overstatement collapses passes while leaving the understating path untouched.

THE SINGLE-MODEL FIXTURE TRAP. The local lane serves exactly one model, so a fixture built from configured lanes cannot express the model defect at all. The model survives today only because the lane's --settings payload carries a modelPicker with replaceBuiltInOptions true offering one option; nothing in the code preserves it. At the current HEAD I measured: _repository_scope_claims is 67 of 73 seconds; it calls _resolved_scope_entries 43 times, which calls runs.py _project_derivations 31 times, once per live pointer; each of those calls _store.read_plan then compose_project_state, and inside compose_project_state _hydrate_items costs 28.5 of 28.8 seconds because _plan_state_by_slug parses every plan HTML in the project. Across five mounted repositories one dispatch ran _plan_html.read_state 285 times. Confirm the shape still holds before repairing; the absolute seconds will differ on your run and are not the measure. The mechanism is that _project_derivations wants only the small derivations mapping, which lives in the composed project manifest, and pays for every sprint item hydration to get it. Repair it so the derivation map is read without hydrating plan state. If you add a memo, key it on a file signature the way project_state._plan_file_signature does, never on project name alone, because this code also runs inside a long-lived server process where a name-keyed cache goes stale and serves a deleted derivation forever. MEASURE BY THE MECHANISM, NOT THE CLOCK: a wall-time bound is a moving number and must not appear in an assertion. The falsifier is a test that counts calls to reckon._plan_html.read_state while resolving scope claims across a synthesised fixture carrying several projects, several plans each, and several live pointers, and requires that number to be independent of the number of live pointers. Range it over the input domain rather than over today's inventory: the test must fail if the count grows with pointer count, which is precisely what it does today. Two positive controls, both required, because a reader that returns nothing is trivially fast: the derivation mapping returned for a project that HAS derivations is byte-identical to what compose_project_state returns for it today, and a project with no derivations still returns an empty mapping rather than raising. Build the fixture in a temp directory and assert the real crew home and the real docs directories are untouched afterwards. Do not report an absolute green; that cohort carries pre-existing failures.

So the comment's who names the worker for a comment the worker did not write. A promotion re-run carrying a corrected outcome therefore finds the stale comment, reports success, and writes nothing. Make a differing body visible to the caller rather than silently discarded; whether it updates the comment or refuses is your design call, but state which you chose and why, and a caller must be able to tell the two cases apart. Falsifiers, both required to fail before the repair and pass after. One: a comment written through the coordinator path carries a who identifying the coordinator's write rather than the run's member, while a comment the worker authored in its own committed plan still attributes to the worker. Two: calling the writer twice under one run id with two DIFFERENT narratives does not report an unqualified success on the second call with the first body still in place. Positive controls that must not regress: an unchanged re-promotion is still idempotent and still writes nothing, and the four-attempt version-conflict retry loop still resolves a concurrent write. Build every fixture in a temp directory and assert the real docs directories and the real crew home are untouched afterwards, since this module writes to both. node_definition.done_when: Reproduce first and quote the reproduction in your manifest. In a temporary git repository, call ledger.register_member twice: once at the default (no commit) for one member, then with commit=True for a second. At the current HEAD the resulting commit's subject names only the second member while its content carries both, because git commit --only snapshots the file's current content rather than the caller's own change. I reproduced this directly and the commit read 'chore(roster): register public-b' over a diff naming internal-a and public-b. That is the defect this plan exists to remove, one level down: a commit whose message describes one change and whose content carries two. Repair it. Two designs are defensible and the choice is yours to make and to state: commit the roster as found but name every registration the commit actually carries, or refuse to commit while the roster holds an uncommitted write the caller did not make and say which write is in the way. Do not silently drop the other write and do not stage a partial file. Falsifier, which must fail at base and pass after: after the two-registration sequence above, the commit's own content and its message agree about which members it carries. The reviewer's second finding is the reason this is being asked for separately, so honour it: the existing fixture always starts from a clean repository and therefore cannot see this at all, so your new case must start from a repository whose roster already holds an uncommitted registration. Positive controls, all required: a single public add on a clean roster still commits exactly one member with a subject naming it; the default path still writes without committing; and an unrelated dirty file elsewhere in the checkout is neither staged nor committed. Build every fixture in a temp directory and assert the real checkout is untouched afterwards. Gate: PYTHONPATH=$PWD /home/ITER/mcintos/Code/reckon/.venv/bin/python -m pytest -p no:cacheprovider -q tests/test_roster_write_commits.py tests/test_ledger.py plus the roster and member asserting files, on a debug partition with --time 00:59:00, captured to one log and reported as added failures against your base sha rather than as an absolute green.
