node_definition.done_when: Read the plan section with read_plan(view='section', section='s4') before starting; it is the authority. The metadata index rows (reckon/metadata_index.py) gain each plan's open-followup count and implementable-section count. Each row is revalidated by one stat of its plan file on every call, and only a plan whose stat identity moved is parsed again. runs._project_executable_remainder reads those rows. Record the base arm first: on the real repository, in a fresh process, time runs._project_executable_remainder('reckon') at base and at head, writing both figures to a log in the run directory as measurement, not as a test assertion; the plan's target is under 0.5 s at head, against a base of about 19.7 s plus 3.0 s of meta parsing. In a new tests/test_drain_reads_the_index.py, built on a synthesised project of 200 plans under the test's temporary path and a temporary configuration home (never the real index or the real configuration home): the remainder computed from the index equals the remainder computed by calling read_state on every plan (the parity case); a second call with no plan changed calls read_state for no plan; after the content of one plan changes, read_state is called at most once, for that plan only. read_state is counted by patching. The named negative control (the remainder reading read_state for every plan again) is executed and fails the no-plan-changed case. The gate is the new test plus tests/test_metadata_index_survives_restart.py, tests/test_page_paints_from_the_index.py and every existing test file under tests/ that calls runs.drain or _project_executable_remainder, run at base and at head; list them in the manifest. The head arm adds no failure id; any added id means status blocked, naming each id. ruff check and ruff format --check over the changed Python paths report no finding the base did not. node_definition.done_when: Read the plan section with read_plan(view='section', section='s4') first; it is the authority. Today recovery.classify_pointer costs about 8.4 s over 12 pointers in a cold obligations call, and _backends.observe_log and parse_events re-parse whole worker streams (about 4.2 s). After the change, the memo is persisted in a file beside each pointer, under the live pointer directory, and its key covers every file the classification reads. The pointer, manifest, stream and review record are the files known today; establish the full set by reading the code, and list it in the manifest. Stream observation resumes from a byte offset persisted in the same memo file. A memo whose key no longer matches is recomputed, never served. Record the base arm first: time obligations('reckon', 's21-1c') in a fresh process at base and at head, into a log under the run directory, as measurement only. In a new tests/test_pointer_classification_is_memoised.py, built on synthesised pointers, manifests and streams under the test's temporary path and a temporary configuration home: a second classification with no input changed does not call parse_events (patched to count); appending to one pointer's stream re-observes only the appended bytes, and only that pointer is reclassified; changing any one input file (manifest, review record, pointer) reclassifies that pointer; and the memoised and uncached classifications agree for every pointer (the parity case). The named negative control (the memo key without the review record) is executed and fails the review-record-changed case. Keep the change inside classify_pointer, its stream observation and the memo; another live node edits obligations._held_worktrees. The gate is the new test plus every existing test file under tests/ that calls classify_pointer, observe_log or observe_stream, run at base and at head with -n 8 and --timeout=300; list them in the manifest. Each arm is recorded as JSON carrying completed true and a literal command with absolute paths and no angle-bracket placeholder. Each log names its revision on the first line and ends with a bare line reading EXIT= followed by the exit code. Every pytest process uses a basetemp private to that process. The head arm adds no failure id; any added id means status blocked, naming each id. ruff check and ruff format --check over the changed Python paths report no finding the base did not. Scratch goes under /tmp in a directory named for this run and is deleted before status complete. An evidence fragment at docs/evidence/fragments/the-obligations-hook-reads-a-snapshot/pointer-classification-is-memoised.html records the change and both timings. The turn ends once the manifest reads complete or blocked.

node_definition.done_when: Read the plan section with read_plan(view='section', section='s2') before starting; it is the authority. The followup's invocation is its prompt field, with recommends_skill as the fallback, in the grammar /reckon-VERB TARGET optionally followed by a section sign and a number. TARGET is a bare slug, project:slug or a sprint id. The section number maps to the section id s plus that number. A followup is a pointer when TARGET names a plan other than its host, a plan in another mount, or a sprint, or when it names its host plan together with a section that the host's section_declarations classify implementable. Anything else hides work, with a reason word from a fixed set that distinguishes no-section, section-not-implementable, host-complete and unparseable. The roadmap finding is emitted next to _unwired_plan_findings in reckon/roadmap.py through the existing _finding helper. It covers every plan the roadmap inventories, including completed ones, and names the plan, the followup id and the reason word. No other module re-implements the classification. In a new tests/test_a_followup_that_hides_work_is_found.py, built on plans written into a temporary docs directory (never the real docs tree or configuration home), assert the predicate's answer and reason for five cases: a pointer to another plan, a pointer to the host's implementable section, a followup naming a done section, a followup naming no section, and a followup on a shipped plan naming its host. Assert also that the roadmap's findings list exactly the three that hide work. Execute the named negative control and confirm the no-section case fails. Then run the predicate over the real /home/ITER/mcintos/Code/reckon/docs/plans read-only and write a log in the run directory with the count by reason word, plus every followup id the plan's section 1 counted as hiding work (102 rows) that the predicate calls a pointer, or the reverse, each with its reason. The gate is the new test plus every existing test file under tests/ that imports reckon.roadmap or calls roadmap(, found by a text search; run it at base and at head and list the files in the manifest. Each arm is recorded as JSON carrying completed true and a literal command with absolute paths and no angle-bracket placeholder. Each log names its revision on the first line and ends with a bare line reading EXIT= followed by the exit code. Every pytest process uses a basetemp private to that process, outside any repository. The head arm adds no failure id; any added id means status blocked, naming each id. ruff check and ruff format --check over the changed Python paths report no finding the base did not. Scratch goes under /tmp in a directory named for this run and is deleted before status complete. An evidence fragment at docs/evidence/fragments/work-is-a-section-not-a-followup/predicate-and-finding.html records the change, the real-tree counts and the disagreements. The turn ends once the manifest reads complete or blocked.

node_definition.done_when: §11 asks for the producer's CPU over the measured nine-worker shape, read with pidstat for 60 s, before and after. The measured baseline is 60 to 66 percent of a core on 2026-09-24. Both arms run on the fleet allocation in a temporary RECKON_HOME, never against the live reckon producer or ~/.config/reckon. A driver synthesises nine live run pointers whose stream.jsonl files each grow at a steady rate of about 2 MB over the window, using realistic assistant and tool records. For each arm it reads pidstat -u 1 60 on the producer's own process id (or utime+stime deltas from that process's /proc stat file when pidstat is absent) and records mean and peak %CPU. It also records 8 s of strace -c -f read/openat counts where strace is available, the revision each arm imported (asserted from module __file__), the growth rate and the run count. A report producer-cpu.md in the run directory, copied to ~/.config/reckon/crew/reports/reckon/, states both figures and the ratio; the driver, both logs and the pidstat outputs stay in the run directory. Every producer the driver started is stopped by pid and listed, and none outlives the node.
